An example reason for a high Growth score: posting to an internal Tech blog received more than 100 reactions, producing a tangible sense of accomplishment.

A practical self-reflection method for identifying personal psychological needs involves listing what has been fulfilled versus unfulfilled in categories such as achievement/competence, relatedness, and existence, then combining those observations with specific background events to generate hypotheses about one's deeper desires.
Example of competence/achievement fulfillment: Completing a latency-reduction project that successfully halved p95 latency.

Example of relatedness deficit: Code-review requests left unaddressed for more than a week, plus receiving company-wide positive reactions to a blog post while receiving zero reactions from one's own team.
Example of existence (basic well-being) deficit: Recurring nighttime alerts that produced mid-week sleep deprivation.

Derived insight from the example: Even when one receives recognition from the broader organization, the absence of any reaction from the immediate team can produce a felt lack of relatedness, revealing that the individual actually seeks strong interpersonal connection within the team.
By systematically writing out fulfillment status and pairing it with concrete events, a person can become consciously aware of the specific needs they are seeking to satisfy.

The Achievement Matrix (達成感マトリクス) is a simple visualization tool for engineers to numerically identify and understand what types of work give them a sense of accomplishment, supporting daily motivation management.

To create an Achievement Matrix: (1) Enumerate work categories you are involved in, such as feature development, non-functional development, product quality improvement, code quality improvement, bug fixes, and incident response. (2) For each category, rate the sense of accomplishment on a 1–5 scale (higher = stronger sense of achievement) at three stages: start/着手時, execution/実行時, and completion/完了時. (3) Verbalize the qualitative feeling of that achievement in a short sentence.

Example Achievement Matrix for an engineer who finds fulfillment in feature development: Feature development scores 4 (start), 4 (execution), 5 (completion) with the quality description 'Implemented a new screen that users can use intuitively, and received cheers during the internal demo.'

In the same example, non-functional development scores 3-4-4: 'Benchmark numbers improved visibly, and the entire backend team did a fist pump.' Product quality improvement scores 2-3-3: 'Conducted A/B testing and gained a sense of security by verifying user experience numerically, but it was a quiet satisfaction without flashiness.'

Code quality improvement in the example scores 3-3-4: 'Performed refactoring; nesting became shallower and readability improved. Felt like a gift to my future self.' Bug fixes score 2-4-4: 'The moment the error cause was identified brought a refreshing “mystery solved” feeling; user impact was immediately resolved.'

Incident response in the example scores lowest at 1-2-3: 'Fatigued from late-night work, but felt relief when the service recovery alert stopped. More fatigue than heroism.' This contrast helps reveal personal motivation patterns across different engineering tasks.

The Achievement Matrix (達成感マトリクス) is a tool for engineers to meta-cognitively analyze their motivation by rating different work categories on a scale (typically 1-5) across three phases: start (着手時), execution (実行時), and completion (完了時), then verbalizing the quality of the sense of achievement.

Example ratings for an engineer who finds fulfillment in quality improvement: Feature development scores 2/3/3 — positive user reactions are nice but increasing technical debt is concerning; Non-functional development scores 3/4/4 — reduced cache miss rates and clear performance gains feel good because invisible improvements are satisfying; Product quality improvement scores 3/3/3 — completing logic fixes requested by multiple users is good but it should have been considered from the initial development; Code quality improvement scores 4/4/5 — replacing a legacy API and eliminating a long-standing bottleneck provides strong fulfillment from exercising engineering skills; Bug fixes score 2/3/4 — fixing the bug itself brings achievement but starting is frustrating because ideally bugs shouldn't be introduced; Incident response scores 3/3/3 — resolving a state that damages customer value is necessary and completing it is good, but there may have been insufficient prior verification.

By examining actual development work through this matrix, engineers can discover their personal motivation sources, achieve meta-cognition of themselves, and consciously practice motivation management.

Personal OKRs should be linked to an engineer's own desires/needs (欲求). For a numerical target like 'reduce p90 latency of first request from 1500ms to 800ms', explicitly clarify how it relates to personal desires.

When an organization uses OKRs, such metrics typically connect to customer value, e.g., Objective: Overwhelming UX improvements that make customers want to keep using the product; Key Results: Reduce p90 latency of first request from 1500ms to 800ms.

When an organizational OKR does not fully motivate you, keep the Key Result (what to do / what to measure) unchanged but rephrase the Objective (the reason for doing it) to align with your personal desires. This creates a personal Objective alongside the organizational one without replacing the organization's Objective.

Example of personalizing an Objective: If the KR is 'reduce p90 latency of first request from 1500ms to 800ms', someone seeking relatedness might set a personal Objective of 'be recognized by peers as a lead engineer', while someone seeking growth might set 'become able to independently achieve difficult latency reductions'.

Linking an organizational Objective (e.g., customer value) to a personal Objective via the same Key Result can feel unusual when diagrammed, but it is worthwhile if it effectively fuels personal motivation.

Visible representation of progress, such as through dashboards, is important for building a sense of achievement and thus boosting motivation. New feature development naturally allows seeing working results, which supports this visibility.

Performance improvements and test infrastructure work in software development often lack immediately tangible results, making it hard to feel a sense of achievement and thereby negatively impacting developer motivation.

Dashboarding of metrics is an effective countermeasure: making development-environment performance visible at a glance or graphically representing test-execution rates provides a strong motivational boost.

Concrete example: an engineer who had been unable to make progress on test development became highly motivated the same day a progress dashboard was introduced, exclaiming that being able to see the progress was excellent and generated real drive.
Visible, at-a-glance results create a sense of accomplishment that is a powerful driver of human motivation; the practice is therefore worth adopting.
Cross-cutting (horizontal) connections can be fostered by launching theme-based guilds that span teams—covering frontend, backend, QA, DevOps, cloud, etc.

Activities such as Lightning-Talk (LT) sessions or informal discussions of shared challenges, held in a setting slightly removed from day-to-day product work, reduce isolation and strengthen organizational solidarity.

Cross-team 1-on-1 meetings and mentorship (called 'diagonal relationships') are effective because they allow people to discuss concerns they cannot raise with a direct supervisor due to conflicting interests. Having someone in the company who understands you helps satisfy the need for relatedness.
A manager's work is often aimed at medium-to-long-term outcomes, making it hard to feel short-term accomplishment and easy to question the meaning of one's current actions.

Managers should record their daily actions (e.g., conducting interviews, recommending hiring candidates, planning technical-debt repayment, appointing tech leads, stakeholder coordination, member 1-on-1s) in a regular habit such as a daily or weekly report.

When a team measures engagement, mapping the manager's recorded actions onto the six-month engagement trend lets the manager infer which actions had positive or negative effects, even though engagement is influenced by multiple variables and cannot be attributed to a single action.

Managers working with a mid-to-long-term perspective inevitably experience 'blank periods of accomplishment' (手応えの空白期間) because roadmap milestones and organizational change outcomes typically only become visible after a quarter, half-year, or full year.
If the 'fuel of achievement' runs out during these blank periods, the manager's own motivation can waver and a sense of stagnation can propagate to the entire team.
Quick Wins (クイックウィン) are small, fast, and reliably value-delivering results that managers should intentionally embed into long-term work to periodically recharge the sense of achievement.
Quick Wins are not a substitute for abandoning long-term goals; they function as auxiliary supports (補助線) that help maintain the stamina needed to pursue those long-term goals.
Effective Quick Wins for managers should satisfy three conditions: (1) completable within one week, (2) value that can be visualized immediately, and (3) a clear connection to the long-term goal.

Example application: In a team's development process involving integration-test specification reviews, introducing a generative AI tool to produce external specification documents can serve as a Quick Win that meets the three conditions.
Figure 1.20 illustrates a timeline that maps team engagement levels against the specific actions taken by the manager.

Adding AI-based matching/verification (突合) can be executed via relatively lightweight tasks such as deciding which prompts to use, confirming local operation, and creating guidelines on what to delegate to AI versus what humans should judge.
Delegating some previously human judgments to AI produces a clearly visible value: shortened work time.
Development-process improvements directly raise team development productivity and therefore connect to long-term goals.

Additional effective actions for motivation management include hosting lunchtime Lightning Talk (LT) sessions to cultivate team learning habits and building dashboards for the metrics a manager wants to monitor.
A secondary effect of delivering a quick win is that members gain trust, thinking “that manager actually gets their own hands dirty.”
Even when a manager is no longer writing large amounts of code, contributing directly to the field remains a meaningful action.
Horizontal connections that allow one to realize 'one's worries are not unique to oneself' serve as the greatest source of energy.

Nurturing relationships to learn together with peers tackling the same challenges, crossing organizational walls and company boundaries, simultaneously satisfies Relatedness needs (R) and Growth needs (G).
Cross-cutting connections are important not only for engineers but also for managers, and such connections extend beyond the company as well.
Numerous communities exist, including those specialized by programming language, those focused on Agile/Scrum, and even separate communities for experts versus beginners within the same genre.

Although it takes courage to join a community for the first time, it provides opportunities to learn about universal challenges existing beyond company frameworks and to connect with peers who share similar real-life concerns.
Connecting within communities and challenging oneself to disseminate information there contributes to fulfilling growth needs and relatedness needs.

The author's impetus for sharing about OKR originated from community activities and dialogues; observing that many workplaces were adopting OKR but struggling with how to make it work, the author shared their own site experiences, exchanged opinions, brought insights back to practice, which ultimately led to writing the book 'アジャイルチームによる目標づくりガイドブック'.
When struggling and suffering because work in front of one is not going well, communities provided warm support and the courage to move forward again.
Because members do not belong to the same company, the 'diagonal relationship' allows speaking with a sense of security, and thus enables pushing each other's backs.
Seek out companions who mutually 'light each other's fire' (火を灯し合う仲間).
Task management and time management are both essential for building one's career and for completing assigned work.
Task Management is defined as organizing the things that need to be done (やるべきことの整理).
Time Management is defined as designing how much time can be allocated to the things that need to be done (やるべきことにどれだけ時間を配分できるかの設計).
Task management and time management must be treated together because they are inseparable; they interlock like gears and only exert power when they mesh.
A well-organized and prioritized task list is meaningless if dedicated, focused time for those tasks is not secured.
Securing time without deciding what to work on results in waste.
Some actions serve as both task management and time management at once, such as clarifying what not to do in order to free up time.

Motivation is the driving force that enables engineers to keep producing value, but even a full tank of motivation is ineffective if the path forward is congested; time must be controlled so that motivation can be converted into results.

Time management analogy: A congested road preventing progress toward a destination represents work states where engineers and managers cannot advance due to packed schedules, frequent context-switching from concurrent duties (high switching costs), and constant interruptions from chats or notifications.
Typical manager experience: Calendars completely filled with meetings leave no dedicated time for actual focused work, leading to frustration.
Daily work consists of two mixed types of time: (1) concentrated value-creation time that requires deep focus, and (2) fragmented peripheral-task time that is frequently interrupted.
Consequence of interruptions: Notifications during deep-concentration work cause the mental structures being built to collapse, forcing a complete restart the next day.

Outcome of poor time management: Spending an entire day feeling busy yet being unable to identify any completed accomplishments, resulting only in fatigue (a classic frustration from lacking time management).
Core principle: Time is a precious asset granted equally to everyone; the ability to manage it properly determines success in producing results, personal growth, and enjoying life.
Chapter context: This material introduces Chapter 2 on Task and Time Management, using the congestion metaphor (Figure 2.1) to illustrate why effective time allocation is essential.
Time management is not merely a technique for using limited time efficiently; its essence is the skill of intentionally creating 'margin' (余白).

'Margin' (余白) does not mean simply leaving the calendar empty. It means intentionally leaving spare time and cognitive capacity (without using 100% of resources such as schedule and cognitive resources) that can be directed toward change, learning, inspection, and adaptation.
Time management is conceptualized as 'the technique of designing margin'.

Traffic-jam analogy: When congestion occurs, the required action is not to press the accelerator harder (which would cause a major accident) but to secure space that allows detours or stopping in order to avoid or resolve the congestion.
The same principle applies to engineering work: the higher the utilization rate becomes due to scheduled work and interruptions, the harder it is for important work to make progress.
Therefore the core of time management is not packing more tasks into the schedule but designing margin so that congestion can be resolved or avoided.

Once a goal is set, one approach is to keep heading toward it continuously; the alternative is to periodically stop, check whether the goal has changed, and adapt if it has (illustrated as Figure 2.2: keep going straight versus stop and change direction).

This book treats two kinds of slack (余白): (1) time slack (時間の余白) — deliberately avoiding packed schedules so that time remains for unexpected interruptions and for deliberation; (2) cognitive slack (認知の余白) — reducing the occupation of attention and working memory so that thinking capacity remains.
Both forms of slack constitute the foundation that supports the capacity to adapt to change; that adaptive capacity is a primary source of competitiveness in modern knowledge work.

Markets and technologies now shift on monthly, weekly, or even daily timescales rather than yearly ones; therefore the ability to secure time to pause and change direction determines whether results can be sustained.

Since the Industrial Revolution, prevailing labor ideology has prized maximization of utilization rates—an idea that originated in factories and manufacturing and was later imported unchanged into knowledge work. Consequently slack has been treated as something that impairs efficiency and therefore ought to be eliminated.

Although there is now some movement to reconsider excessive efficiency, many organizations and individuals still operate with the mindset that any emerging slack must immediately be filled with more work.
As a result, conventional time management is typically framed as the art of ‘somehow juggling things so as to squeeze out extra time.’
Slack (余白) is often misunderstood as laziness; merely understanding this is insufficient. One must deepen understanding of the value slack creates, then change mindset and actions accordingly.

Practical slack-creating actions include inserting a 10-minute buffer between meetings and fixing a weekly 60-minute slot to review plans and priorities. These are necessary actions for following change, not slacking.
Three core values of slack emphasized: adaptation to change, acquisition of creativity, and avoidance of burnout.
Slack provides the leeway needed to change direction when circumstances shift.

Comparison of planning approaches: a detailed 3-month plan executed strictly versus pausing weekly to review and adjust the plan. Changes begin spreading impact immediately upon occurrence, so early inspection and adaptation are desirable.

If the inspection interval is larger than the frequency of changes, work accumulates in a misaligned state and rework becomes large. In frequently changing environments, weekly reviews enable far better following of change.
This difference also appears in the contrast between resource efficiency and flow efficiency.
Resource efficiency: the mindset of pursuing a state in which each individual resource (people or machines) is always operating at 100% utilization.
Flow efficiency: the mindset of making the entire work flow smooth so that the time until value reaches the customer is minimized.

Resource efficiency (リソース効率) optimizes for a state where 'everyone is constantly moving their hands' (全員が常に手を動かしている状態). This results in progressing many things simultaneously, which necessitates coordination and adjustment, leading to the creation of meetings and regular check-ins (会議や定例).

Flow efficiency (フロー効率) emphasizes the 'lead time to deliver value' (価値を届けるためのリードタイム). It involves completing one job before starting the next and reducing the number of in-progress items known as WIP (Work In Progress).
In flow efficiency, the critical goal is shortening the lead time required to deliver value, not maximizing the number of in-progress jobs that can be held.
Reducing the number of in-progress jobs (WIP) in order to shorten lead time for value delivery consequently creates slack or margin (余白). This slack provides strength and resilience against changes.

The Toyota Production System's Kanban system and Lean development philosophy place high importance on maintaining slack (余白を持たせること). This approach enables rapid switching even if specification changes or priority shifts occur midway.

Although 100% utilization might allow for top speed, in highly variable or changing environments, the ability to frequently change direction (こまめに方向転換できる) results in a shorter overall time to reach the goal.

Figure 2.3 illustrates the contrast between resource efficiency and flow efficiency from the perspective of WIP (Work In Progress), showing multiple simultaneous WIP items under resource efficiency versus fewer under flow efficiency.

Tom DeMarco stated in 'Slack' that 'slack is the degree of freedom for change, and without it, organizations become rigid.' In environments like software development where the speed of change is extremely fast, this degree of freedom is a lifeline.

Having slack to pause for a change of direction also leads to personal growth. Most teams the author has been involved with plan in small weekly increments, inspect the results, and adapt. Each week they reflect on events and consider 'how can we become better?' then take action.
Reflecting and taking action on one's behavior every week creates approximately 50 opportunities for change and growth in a year.

The ability to change direction means having the leeway to try new possibilities. Slack is indispensable not only for the defensive purpose of 'following change' but also for the offensive purpose of 'creating new value.'

Creativity is born by newly combining existing knowledge and experience. This 'combinatorial thinking' requires time to digest and associate information. When a schedule is packed, this process does not function. Slack gives the brain room to perform combinatorial thinking and becomes the soil that produces unexpected insights.
To exercise creativity, it is necessary to keep antennas up across a wide range of areas on a daily basis and store various information in one's own drawer.

Google's '20% rule' was a system in which employees could spend 20% of their week on projects based on their own interests. It is well known that innovative services such as Gmail were born from this. This is an excellent example of slack directly generating new value.

In the author's workplace, during periods such as year-end and New Year when planning is more difficult than usual, they sometimes boldly refrain from making plans and set aside a 'free research' period in which each member commits to things they normally want to do but have not been able to.

In periods of available time (margin), individuals demonstrate creativity by building tools to rapidly set up personal development environments, challenging themselves with implementations of new algorithms, or creating experimental chatbots leveraging generative AI.
Simply completing scheduled tasks without margin leads to physical and mental exhaustion.
The World Health Organization (WHO) defines burnout as 'a syndrome conceptualized as resulting from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed.'

Burnout syndrome tendencies include: Exhaustion (depletion of energy and a completely worn-out feeling), Cynicism (emotional distancing from work and a negative attitude), and Inefficacy (reduced sense of accomplishment and lowered confidence in one's abilities).

Some individuals may consciously choose a path of complete burnout, analogous to the protagonist Yabuki Joe in the manga 'Ashita no Joe' (1967–1973), who fights until only white ash remains; the author does not condemn those who elect this, noting that life itself may exist to be fully expended.
Unintentional burnout, however, should be avoided.

Primary causes of burnout include: heavy responsibility pressure (results expectations, personnel development, evaluations, and conflict resolution creating high mental load); loneliness (difficulty speaking honestly with superiors or subordinates and lack of a confidant); role ambiguity (diverse or contradictory expected roles with unclear success criteria); lack of recognition (few opportunities for acknowledgment or evaluation); and normalization of self-sacrifice (chronic long hours and team-first thinking that postpones self-care).
Moderate yohaku (margin/slack/white space) prevents the normalization of self-sacrifice, providing mental and physical leeway that keeps people from burning out like ashes.
The foundation for preventing burnout is the daily securing of yohaku (margin), even though burnout itself is covered in detail in Chapter 3.
Even when tasks are clearly defined and unchanging, it is not advisable to maximize resource efficiency by using 100% of available resources.

System analogy for resources: If a system's CPU usage is constantly at 100%, new incoming requests cannot be processed in time, tasks pile up in a queue, responses become slow, and from the user's perspective the system appears 'not working'.
CPU usage has a 'stable operation zone (with margin)' versus a 'danger zone' at 100% utilization (illustrated in Figure 2.4).
Memory analogy: If a program continuously allocates more memory than needed, garbage collection (GC) occurs more frequently, degrading performance.
Key principle titled 'リソースを使い切らない' (Do not use up all resources): leave unused capacity as a buffer rather than operating at full utilization.
Mechanisms that maintain system health (like garbage collection or memory management) are essential, but if they trigger too frequently, performance drops significantly.
Human brains and computers are not identical, but they share a similarity: processing capacity has an upper limit, and operating near that limit causes waiting and switching costs to surge.
Overloading with information or schedules forces extra energy expenditure on switching and organizing, reducing resources available for actual work.

Psychological research on task switching has repeatedly observed 'switch costs': immediately after switching tasks, reactions become slower and errors increase. (Reference: Trends Cogn Sci, 2003 Mar;7(3):134-140)

Increased switching costs mean that even with the same total work hours per day, the time convertible into actual deliverables decreases. Each switch from task A to B requires re-understanding, re-planning, and re-exploration, reducing pure progress.
As a result, the number of tasks completable per unit time (effective throughput) tends to decrease. Lower throughput in turn makes 'waiting' more likely.

Little's Law from queueing theory provides an approximation for the relationship between waiting time and work-in-progress: Average number of customers (L) = Arrival rate (λ) × Average sojourn time (W). This holds when the system is stable and long-term averages can be defined. (Reference: John D. C. Little, 1961, A Proof for the Queuing Formula: L = λW. Operations Research 9(3):383-387)
Example of Little's Law: If a bank or hospital counter has 10 people arriving per hour (λ=10) and an average of 30 people waiting (L=30), then average sojourn time per person (W) is 3 hours.
Little's Law holds independently of queue form or distribution under a wide range of conditions, making it widely applicable across fields.
Rewritten for engineering work: Average sojourn/residence time = Average work-in-progress (WIP) ÷ Average throughput.

Little's Law applied to engineering work: Average Lead Time = Average WIP (Work In Progress) / Average Throughput. Average WIP is the number of tasks being handled in parallel; average throughput is the number of tasks that can be processed per unit time.

The more concurrent tasks (WIP) you carry, the longer it inevitably takes for any single task to finish. Conversely, reducing WIP shortens average lead time. This is why taking on too many tasks slows overall progress.
Deliberately leaving slack and controlling the number of in-progress items actually maximizes throughput.

Humans overloading their schedules is analogous to running a CPU at constant 100% load and stacking tasks in a queue: it increases waiting time and context-switching costs. Leaving slack reduces WIP and restores a smooth flow.
To create slack, one must first identify 'time thieves' that steal personal time, referencing the gray men in Michael Ende's novel Momo who persuade people to save time.

In Michael Ende's 'Momo', a key quote illustrates the grey men's philosophy: 'Whether work is enjoyable or whether one works with love for the job is no longer an issue—rather, such thoughts become obstacles to work. The only important thing is to do as much work as possible in as short a time as possible.'

People trapped by this mindset include a barber who eliminated conversations with customers as 'wasted time' and cityscapes that become uniform in the name of efficiency; time is saved but '心の余白' (mental/heart margin or inner space) is stolen, leading to a loss of richness.

This depiction of false efficiency stealing human margin resonates deeply with modern life, where unnoticed '時間どろぼう' (time thieves) erode concentration and inner space even as they appear to create more free time.
The book distinguishes two types of 余白 (margin/white space): '時間の余白' (time margin) and '認知の余白' (cognitive margin).

Time thieves in this context include not only things that directly steal clock time but also those that occupy attention and working memory, thereby reducing cognitive margin and indirectly eroding time margin.

Organizing cognitive margin does not necessarily add empty slots to a calendar immediately, but it reduces losses from hesitation, reconfirmation, and context-switching, which in the long run restores time margin.
Common modern time thieves include fragmented schedules and constant notifications; the book personifies frequently encountered time thieves as characters to make them identifiable.
The 'Anaboko Kozō' (Hole-Poking Kid) is a metaphorical thief that disrupts concentration by scattering meetings throughout the schedule, creating small 'puddles' that prevent deep focus.
This disruption commonly appears when someone is concurrently assigned to multiple teams or when their team is large.
Even a small number of meetings (e.g., only three) can ruin productivity if they are poorly placed, fragmenting the remaining time into unusable scraps.
Example of fragmented schedule: a 30-minute meeting at 10 AM, a 1-hour meeting at 1 PM, and a 45-minute meeting at 4 PM leaves only broken intervals that cannot support deep work.
Humans require time to enter a concentrated state known in psychology as 'flow'; typically 15–20 minutes of uninterrupted immersion is needed (with individual variation).
A 30-minute meeting inserted into a one-hour block forces the worker to restart the concentration process twice, consuming most of the available time and leaving only miscellaneous tasks completed.
The resulting subjective experience is that 'nothing substantial got done today' despite few meetings, because the placement rather than the quantity of meetings is the real problem.
The 'Piko-Piko Ninja' (ピコピコ忍者) is a metaphor for constant, distracting notifications that sneak into the brain and plant small seeds of distraction, stealing focus from intended work.

Even when work time is reserved for a specific task, being at the mercy of the Piko-Piko Ninja (checking notifications) can cause the entire work block to vanish, leaving one facing the next meeting with nothing accomplished.

Example: While concentrating on writing code, a Slack notification appears. Opening it reveals a low-priority message that could have waited. The interruption breaks the work rhythm, and one may end up browsing news sites instead.

The danger of notifications is that fragments of awareness remain in the brain. Even if not immediately acted upon, thoughts like 'I need to reply' or 'I might need to check this' create small 'incomplete' items that occupy working memory.
These notifications generate 'tasks for the sake of tasks' (タスクのためのタスク), which is the truly frightening aspect of the Piko-Piko Ninja.
This concept is part of identifying 'time thieves' (時間どろぼう) in the context of task and time management.
The 'Sitting Goblin' (居座りゴブリン) is a metaphor for unfinished or in-progress tasks that occupy a corner of the mind; it whispers 'don't forget' even when idle and hijacks thinking.
The Sitting Goblin appears when task sizes have not been properly divided or when too many jobs are left in progress at once.
Even people skilled at task division can allow the goblin to occupy their mind during high-uncertainty periods such as the launch of a new project.
Everyday examples of tasks that spin in the head include unfinished documents, meeting preparations, and unreplied emails; this is a common daily experience for many people.
This mental state occurs when in-progress tasks occupy the brain's working memory (ワーキングメモリ).

The goblin remains in the brain even without any physical action; leaving unfinished work in the mind while switching to another task constantly pulls away part of one's attention, preventing concentration and lowering efficiency.
The 'Scroll Witch' (スクロール魔女) is a time thief that sweetly lures users with the phrase 'just 5 minutes' into the infinite scroll of SNS and news, distorting their sense of time without them noticing.

In modern work environments, pursuing the latest information or contacting professional connections inevitably leads to opening SNS or searching online news, making complete avoidance difficult even if SNS use during work is generally discouraged.
SNS and news possess an 'endless flow' (際限のない流れ) that continuously stimulates the brain's reward system.
Each scroll to the next post or news item secretes a small amount of dopamine, which reinforces the desire to keep viewing more content.
This dopamine-driven reinforcement loop makes infinite scrolling a particularly powerful 'time thief' (時間どろぼう) for the brain.
チリ積婆 (Chiri Tsumibaba) is a metaphorical 'thief' that confuses priorities by successively presenting small miscellaneous tasks with the lure 'If you just tidy this up, things will become easier.'

Prioritizing these small chores causes substantial blocks of time to vanish unnoticed, as one ends up carrying many tasks that merely 'would be better to do if possible' and 'look like they can be finished quickly.'
The accumulation of fine-grained tasks generates decision paralysis ('Which one should I start with?') and simultaneously erodes cognitive spare capacity (認知の余白).
チリ積婆 exploits the genuine desire to make work incrementally better and the enthusiasm to polish a product down to the last detail.
Typical examples of such tasks include answering emails that do not actually require a reply and making minor layout adjustments to documents.
The presence of anything immediately visible that 'would be better to do and seems quick to finish' reliably triggers an impulsive start, allowing the thief to succeed.
The Zeigarnik husband (ツァイガルニク夫) is a time thief that sneaks up after work or before bed, flashing emails or chats when one is trying to relax after finishing the day's work.
The Zeigarnik husband is related to the lingering goblin (居座りゴブリン) as a member of the same family of time thieves.
The Zeigarnik effect states that unfinished or interrupted tasks are more easily remembered and continue to occupy attention.
Because of this effect, even during rest, thoughts like 'I have to check this on Monday' or 'Maybe I should respond quickly' persist, stealing mental energy.
The Zeigarnik husband erodes rest time and also steals energy needed for the next day.
The book focuses on classifying six specific time thieves, even though many others exist.
Time thieves are classified by invasion route as external or internal, but most affect both time and cognition (with primary and side effects).

Time thieves that attack from the outside interrupt independently of one's will and directly reduce leftover time (time surplus/margins). Increased interruptions and fragmentation also increase context-switching, which in turn erodes cognitive surplus/margins in a chain reaction.

External time thieves: あなぼこ小僧 (scattered meetings that fragment concentration), ピコピコ忍者 (notifications that break focus), ツァイガルニク夫 (invades after work hours and steals rest). Their common trait is that they rush in from outside so that 'before you know it, time is gone.'

Countermeasures for external time thieves center on arranging the environment: consolidating meetings, turning off notifications, protecting off-time boundaries. The key is closing the invasion routes.

Time thieves that arise from the inside mainly occupy cognitive surplus/margins. The more mental occupancy increases, the more hesitation, re-searching, and re-planning occur, which in turn makes it easier for time itself to be stolen.

Internal time thieves: 居座りゴブリン (unfinished tasks that sit in the mind), スクロール魔女 (voluntarily falling into SNS or news), チリ積婆 (being swept away by small miscellaneous chores). These are 'inner thieves' that arise from within even without external factors.

Example of internal cost: When a 居座りゴブリン is present, every time one starts work it becomes necessary to reconstruct 'what to recall first' and 'what to do next.' Even a few minutes per occurrence, if it happens many times a day, the total time is non-negligible.
Recovering cognitive surplus/margins ultimately increases the time available to move forward.

Countermeasures for internal time thieves consist of changing habits: externalizing tasks to empty the head, restricting SNS, starting with high-priority work, etc. The key is arranging one's own behavioral patterns.
Time thieves (時間どろぼう) can be either external (invading from outside) or internal (arising from within oneself); identifying the type clarifies the path for countermeasures.

Play and recreation are not time thieves. Unintentional, mindless activities like endlessly scrolling SNS (e.g., realizing 30 minutes have passed) are classic time thieves because they steal focus and erode mental space without intention.

Intentional leisure activities chosen by one's own will—such as reading a book, listening to music, watching a movie, or going for a walk—are fundamentally different from leftover-time fillers; they are essential practices for healthy human living.

Research indicates that people who consciously allocate time to hobbies and recreation report higher happiness, greater self-efficacy, and more stable work performance; thus play is an investment that makes time usage more vivid and alive.
Eliminating all play while fighting time thieves is unnecessary and harmful; excessive cutting of recreation leads toward the gray-men world of Momo, where only efficient work remains.
The key distinction is between things that steal time against one's will (thieves, the enemy) and things one deliberately chooses to nourish the heart (play, the ally).
Time thieves are of two types: external ones that invade from outside (prevented by environment design) and internal ones that arise from within (defeated by habit design).
External time thieves invade independently of one's willpower, so changing the environment is the most effective weapon rather than relying on willpower to resist them.
The 'Anaboko Kozo' (hole-digging kid) creates small puddles/gaps in the schedule that trample and disrupt concentration.

Countermeasures against Anaboko Kozo: batch meetings together (e.g., concentrate them in the morning or afternoon), pre-book 'focus blocks' in the calendar, and as a rule refuse meetings that have no agenda.
Key principle against Anaboko Kozo: do not create gaps and instead secure consolidated blocks of time.
The 'Pikopiko Ninja' throws shuriken labeled 'urgent!' or 'emergency!' to scatter attention and cause distraction.

Countermeasures against Pikopiko Ninja: set notification-off times and check messages only at designated intervals, separate work accounts or devices, and switch to a mindset of 'I go and fetch information myself' rather than reacting to incoming items.
Key principle against Pikopiko Ninja: do not react passively; a stance of working based on notifications and incoming contacts quickly puts one at the complete mercy of this thief.
自分の時間に対してオーナーシップを持ち、能動的に行動することが大切である。自分に「お前は何がしたいの？」と問いかけ、自分のハンドルを自分で握ることが重要。
ツァイガルニク効果（未完了のタスクが頭に残り続ける心理現象）は、夜になると「まだ終わってないぞ」と休息を奪う時間どろぼうである。対策は自分で境界線を引くこと。
オンとオフの境界を明確に守るための具体策：就業後に業務アプリを閉じる、夜間の緊急連絡は電話のみとチームルールを決める、通知を自動的にサイレントにする仕組みを導入する。
24時間365日すべてオンコール対応の状態では身が持たない。自分で境界線を引き、その境界線を守るためには周囲との協調・合意が不可欠。
内側から生まれる時間どろぼう（自分の心や習慣から湧き出るもの）は、外側の鍵では防げない。必要なのは習慣のデザインである。
「居座りゴブリン」（頭の中に居座る未完了タスクの記憶）を退治するには、タスクを脳から追い出すこと。具体策：やることはすべて書き出す（外部化）、「次の一歩」まで明確にして書く、一日の終わりにタスクを見直し翌日に持ち越さない。
Do not use your head as a storage place for tasks. Writing down everything in your mind onto a memo or note has a surprisingly powerful effect on productivity and mental clarity.
Break tasks down to a size that can realistically be completed within the same day; small, finishable tasks reduce overwhelm and increase completion rates.

The 'scroll witch' (スクロール魔女) is a metaphor for the habit of being lured by 'just 5 minutes' of scrolling on SNS or news, which then steals your sense of time. Counter it by setting explicit viewing rules rather than trying to abstain completely.

Effective rules against mindless scrolling: restrict SNS/news to specific windows (e.g., lunch break or commuting time only); delete apps to add friction and extra steps for access; replace the habit with alternative rest activities such as stretching or walking.
Combat unconscious scrolling habits with systems and environmental design, not willpower. Accept that the behavior has become automatic and therefore cannot be reliably controlled by intention alone.
The 'dust-accumulation hag' (チリ積婆) is a metaphor for the tendency to accept many small, easy tasks that gradually obscure truly important work. Counter it by consciously prioritizing.
Priority tactics: begin each day with the most important task; batch all miscellaneous work into a dedicated 'misc-task time' slot; cultivate the courage to decide what you will not do.
Advance important (often difficult) work first rather than starting with easy items. This is the 'eat the frog' principle, referenced from Brian Tracy's book 'Eat That Frog!' (2015 Japanese edition).
Overall approach: rely on external systems, written capture, task sizing, time-boxing, and priority sequencing rather than relying on raw willpower to manage attention and productivity.
時間どろぼうを退治するには根性や我慢ではなく「設計」が重要である。外からのどろぼうには侵入経路を閉じる「環境設計」、内からのどろぼうには行動パターンを変える「習慣設計」を施し、どろぼうの正体を見極めてそれぞれに合った対策をとる。
変化への適応には、割り込みを受け止める「時間の余白」だけでなく、状況を理解し判断する「認知の余白」も必要である。どちらの余白が削られているかを見極めて対策を選ぶことが、時間を守り余白を生み出す実践的アプローチとなる。
時間を自らコントロールするには、時間どろぼうを退治するだけでは不十分で、奪われた時間を取り戻すだけでなく能動的に時間を設計することが重要である。どろぼうが入りにくい高いセキュリティの家をつくるように、時間を設計する具体的技術が必要となる。
私たちの時間は通知・会議・雑務などの「時間どろぼう」によって容易に奪われ、気づけば一日が終わっている。これを防ぐには受動的な対処を超え、自ら時間を設計する仕組みが求められる。

The 'flow state' (フロー状態), named and proposed by psychologist M. Csikszentmihalyi, describes the experience of becoming so absorbed in an activity that one loses track of time. In sports, this is sometimes called 'entering the zone' (ゾーンに入る).

Characteristics of being in a flow state include: extremely high concentration (completely focused on the activity, ignoring everything else); loss of self-consciousness (becoming unaware of oneself or others' evaluations, entering a state of total absorption); distortion of time perception (forgetting the passage of time or feeling it pass quickly); clear goals and immediate feedback (knowing exactly what to do and seeing results of one's actions immediately); a sense of control (feeling that one can manage the situation); and the activity itself being rewarding (enjoyable and fulfilling without needing external rewards like money or fame).

Conditions necessary to enter a flow state: engaging with the activity proactively and of one's own volition; being able to immediately see the results of one's actions and easily make course corrections; and having a balance between the challenge level and one's skills.
Actions that improve motivation (as introduced in Chapter 1) also play an important role in inducing the flow state.
To enter a flow state, it is important to push everything other than the current activity out of one's mind, and to secure a reasonably substantial block of time for the activity.

WIP (Work In Progress) refers to in-progress or unfinished work currently occupying your mind. The more WIPs you have, the more mental resources are consumed by thoughts like 'which one should I do next?' or 'I also have to advance that other task...', making it difficult to enter a flow state.
The ideal number of WIPs is 1. Creating a state where only a single task is in your mind allows you to fully immerse yourself and concentrate exclusively on the work in front of you.

In reality, especially for engineers and managers, achieving WIP=1 is difficult. Team development often involves additional simultaneous work such as code reviews for members or sudden inquiry responses alongside one's main implementation tasks.

Time Boxing is a technique to help enter a flow state despite multiple WIPs: you decide a fixed 'time box' in advance (e.g., 'I will work on this task for only 90 minutes'). The predetermined time limit increases concentration and prevents work from dragging on indefinitely.
Example of Time Boxing: Setting 'document creation for 2 hours in the morning' makes you conscious of the end time, which improves both the quality and speed of the output.
By creating a time-limited situation of 'I will concentrate only on this work during this period,' Time Boxing temporarily achieves WIP=1.

The Pomodoro Technique is a specific form of Time Boxing: it consists of 25 minutes of focused work followed by a 5-minute short break, repeated in cycles. The name 'Pomodoro' comes from the Italian word for 'tomato,' originating from the use of a tomato-shaped kitchen timer.
The Pomodoro Technique uses 25-minute focused work intervals, which strike a good balance for exercising concentration without causing excessive exhaustion or fatigue.
The Pomodoro Technique requires only a timer to practice and is widely available via browser extensions, making it a broadly adopted and accessible time-management method.
Starting with the Pomodoro Technique is recommended as an effective first step for learning time-control techniques.
Time Blocking is a method of protecting work time by reserving it in advance as explicit blocks on a calendar.

Time Blocking is especially valuable for manager-type roles that are frequently interrupted by meetings; personal work time will not be protected unless it is booked as a formal 'appointment' or scheduled event.
Example of Time Blocking: pre-schedule blocks such as 'morning for code review' and 'afternoon for document creation' so that colleagues are less likely to interrupt.
Time blocking (タイムブロッキング) should be used cautiously by managers: overfilling the calendar can make it difficult for team members to consult or approach them.

When applying time blocking, form an explicit agreement with collaborating members that certain blocks are reserved for focused work; without this consensus, colleagues may feel it is hard to work together or may interrupt the reserved time anyway.
Calendar defragmentation (カレンダーのデフラグ) is a technique for creating continuous free time by consolidating scattered meetings and appointments rather than letting them fragment the schedule.
The method is presented as a countermeasure to fragmented calendars that leave only small, unusable gaps (referred to as あなぼこ小僧 / 'pothole' holes).

An explicit analogy is drawn to computer hard-disk defragmentation: just as rearranging fragmented data improves performance, rearranging calendar events to cluster meetings produces longer contiguous blocks of usable time.
The recommended practice is therefore to proactively group meetings together so that remaining open slots become substantial, continuous work periods rather than isolated fragments.
Fragmented (fine-grained) time slots force constant task-switching ('what's next?'), imposing a heavy cognitive load known as context switching; this reduces concentration and increases errors.
Consolidating free time via calendar defragmentation (カレンダーをデフラグする) sharply reduces the frequency of context switches.

Consolidated blocks enable entry into a flow state for high-quality, cognitively demanding work such as writing proposals, programming or analysis, allowing uninterrupted deep thinking and higher productivity.
Visible buffer time on the calendar creates psychological slack, lowers chronic time-pressure stress, and supplies a safety margin that lets people handle sudden problems or requests calmly.
A calendar packed only with meetings and micro-tasks produces a purely reactive/passive work style; deliberately inserting vacant blocks shifts the worker toward a proactive, self-directed style.

Creating dedicated time through calendar management enables engagement in higher-value 'proactive' (主体的) activities such as mid-to-long-term planning, developing new ideas, and considering business process improvements.
Calendar defragmentation (カレンダーをデフラグする) is a four-step method to control time and reduce fragmentation of one's schedule.

Step 1 - Grasp current situation and classify tasks (棚卸し/inventory): Review the following week's calendar and color-code all appointments by type (examples: meetings, focused work, small-scale tasks, travel, breaks). This visualization makes time fragmentation immediately apparent.

Step 2 - Group tasks (集約/aggregation): Cluster similar types of tasks together. Examples include designating Thursday as a no-meeting day or setting aside end-of-workday time specifically for small-scale tasks.

Step 3 - Move appointments and negotiate (再配置/rearrangement): Relocate events according to the grouping plan. For meetings that cannot be moved unilaterally, negotiate with counterparts using a positive framing such as 'I would like to secure focused time for better preparation' rather than a simple request to change.

Step 4 - Block and protect focused time (カレンダーの最適化/calendar optimization): Explicitly block the newly created contiguous free time slots on the calendar. Treat these blocks as firm appointments with oneself; leaving them empty invites others to schedule meetings into them. Protecting these blocks is described as the key to success.
The overall approach belongs to Task/Time Management (タスク・タイムマネジメント) and is presented as a practical method for gaining control over one's time (時間をコントロールする方法).

Even when focus or work time is explicitly blocked on a calendar, colleagues may still schedule over it by assuming the block is adjustable; this erosion of intended concentration time should be minimized but not always eliminated entirely.

In team settings, completely isolating one's focus time is not always optimal, because mutual respect for others' situations and a degree of flexibility are required; rigidly optimizing only for oneself can actually reduce overall team productivity.
A practical way to protect personal deep-work time while remaining a good teammate is to apply a gradient (or 'shade') to calendar blocks according to the importance and urgency of the work.

Non-negotiable blocks (absolutely immovable) should be labeled so clearly that anyone looking at the calendar immediately understands they must not interrupt: include the concrete task, the deadline, and an explicit status such as DND (Do Not Disturb). Example notation: 【DND】プルリクレビュー確認（本日中）【作業中・返信不可】.

Adjustable blocks (preferred but open to discussion) should signal flexibility by adding phrases such as '相談OK' (consultation OK) or by listing relatively passive tasks. Example notation: 集中作業（急ぎの際は相談OK）インプット・資料読み込み.
Differentiating the two types of blocks lets the owner retain initiative: instead of having time unilaterally taken, the individual decides whether an adjustment is warranted.
Key principle: '自分が集中できる時間をもつ、チームの生産性にも気を配る' (have time in which you can concentrate, while also paying attention to the team's productivity).

Teams should establish shared rules for securing focused work time, such as agreeing in weekly meetings that each member will block a set number of hours per week for concentrated tasks. This is not merely an individual productivity tactic but a key activity that ultimately raises the quality of the team's overall output.

There is no need to feel guilty about blocking calendar time for one's own focused work. Common team rules remove the psychological barrier, allowing everyone to reserve time confidently and helping to cultivate a culture that respects others' concentration periods.
Once time is secured and a flow state becomes possible, concentrated engagement produces high performance. Properly managing the tasks being worked on further improves the quality of one's work.

To control time effectively, it is essential to make explicit what one actually recognizes as 'work' or tasks: what occupies the mind, what is not being attended to, and what thoughts arise during work.

A powerful method for externalizing the 'things I feel I must do' (unfinished tasks or open loops) from one's mind into a trusted external system is GTD (Getting Things Done), created by David Allen. This keeps the mind clear and raises productivity.
GTD is organized around five core steps (the specific steps themselves are not listed on this page). The term 'Getting Things Done' is a registered trademark of David Allen.
GTD (Getting Things Done) consists of five steps: 1. Collect (収集), 2. Process (処理), 3. Organize (整理), 4. Review (見直し), 5. Execute (実行).
Collect step: Gather every task, commitment, idea, and potential 'thing that might need doing' out of your head into external capture tools such as notes, inboxes, sticky notes, or apps.

Process step: For each captured item ask 'What is it? What is the next action?' Decide whether it is actionable. Non-actionable items are discarded, filed for reference, or placed on a someday/maybe list.
Organize step: Sort processed items into categories, lists, or projects. Separate them by deadline, context, and priority and store them in a trusted system that can be referenced later.
Review step: Regularly (for example a weekly review) examine all task and project lists, update their status, and decide what is finished, what can move forward, and what should be dropped.
Execute step: From the organized and reviewed inventory choose the action that can be done right now and perform it.
The five steps form a continuous cycle (Execute → Review → Organize → Process → Collect).
Core GTD principle: Reduce open loops (unprocessed commitments) that occupy mental bandwidth.
Core GTD principle: Park everything in a trusted external system (inbox, lists, calendar, project tools) so the mind can let go.
Core GTD principle: Every item must have a clearly defined next action; without it motivation collapses.
Following the five steps mechanically is less effective than applying them with an understanding of these underlying principles.

Regular reviews (such as weekly reviews) involve revisiting organized content, deleting unnecessary items, and adjusting priorities; this keeps the GTD system from becoming outdated and prevents mental clutter.
Focus on action by determining when, where, and how to execute each organized task so that it becomes immediately actionable.

GTD Collection phase: Enumerate everything occupying your mind, including unformalized work items (code reviews, tech-blog writing, expense reports, attendance tracking) and personal concerns (unread books, unfinished models, upcoming band practice). Document them messily in a notepad; the goal is to empty the mind, not to structure the list.

GTD Processing phase: Discard items that do not actually need to be done; schedule non-immediate items on a future calendar so they leave current thinking; delegate tasks that others can or should handle; immediately complete any remaining item that takes two minutes or less (e.g., answering a chat mention).
GTD Organize phase: Add the tasks that remain after processing to a personal task list, using tools such as Slack lists or Jira.
GTD Review phase: Classify remaining tasks by priority using the Eisenhower Matrix.
Tasks that remain unstarted despite initial enthusiasm often have unresolved internal hang-ups that should be deeply examined.
The collection and processing steps of task management are especially important because unrecognized tasks gradually steal time; collection visualizes everything without omission.
The processing step of asking 'Should I really do this?' and 'Should I do this now?' often reveals that many current tasks do not actually need to be done by oneself.

The 'Why now?' question, valued by Sequoia Capital, is a key framework for judging priority: when facing interruptions or urgent work, ask what impact would occur if the task were not done now, revealing tasks that can be postponed or delegated.
After applying 'Why now?', use the Eisenhower Matrix (time management matrix) which classifies tasks along two axes: importance and urgency.
The Eisenhower Matrix (アイゼンハワーマトリクス) is a time-management framework that categorizes tasks along two axes: importance (重要度) and urgency (緊急度).
Quadrant 1 (第一領域, top-right): Important and Urgent — these are the highest-priority tasks that must be handled immediately.
Quadrant 2 (第二領域, top-left): Important but Not Urgent — these tasks drive future results and personal/professional growth; they must not be postponed and require deliberate time allocation.
Quadrant 3 (第三領域, bottom-right): Not Important but Urgent — these often consist of interruptions or miscellaneous requests and should be scrutinized with the question “Why now?”
Quadrant 4 (第四領域, bottom-left): Neither Important nor Urgent — these tasks should be deleted or explicitly decided against doing.
Applying the “Why now?” test to reassess urgency and then placing each task in the matrix makes daily decision-making significantly clearer.
Effective task delegation is a strategic act that benefits the delegator, the recipient, and the entire team; it is fundamentally different from merely “dumping work.”

Common psychological barriers to delegation include the beliefs that “I can do it faster and more reliably myself,” “I feel guilty asking a busy colleague,” and “I don’t want to be seen as pushing work onto others.”
Delegation (移譲) creates personal benefit by freeing time to concentrate on higher-value work that only you can perform.
For the recipient, being assigned new or responsible work provides a valuable opportunity for skill development and career growth, while also increasing motivation and a sense of ownership (当事者意識).

For the team, delegation reduces task personalization (属人化, where only specific individuals can perform certain work), thereby raising the team's overall response capability; it also standardizes operations and improves organizational productivity.

In the GTD (Getting Things Done) 'processing' step, any item that would be better handled by someone else should be delegated; this requires asking the question 'Is this something I myself should do?' and transferring tasks answered 'No' in order to increase disposable time and dramatically raise productivity.
Effective delegation begins with correctly identifying which tasks to hand over; the following categories are prime candidates.

Routine/standardized tasks (定型的な業務) such as periodic report creation, data entry, or circulating meeting minutes are the first items to consider for delegation because their procedures are clear and easily documented in manuals.

Tasks outside one's own expertise or areas of weakness (e.g., design work, writing SNS posts, precise data analysis) should be given to team members who excel at them, improving both quality and speed for the whole team.

Work that contributes to the other person's growth (e.g., portions of document creation, leading a small project, sitting in on customer interviews) should be delegated even if slightly challenging, because such stretch assignments directly accelerate development.

Information-gathering and research tasks (e.g., competitor-trend surveys or new-technology scouting) can be delegated once the purpose and desired outcome are clearly communicated, making them accessible even to junior members.
Important-but-not-urgent work (e.g., process-improvement proposals, organizing internal knowledge, or networking) is also suitable for delegation and can introduce fresh perspectives.

Proper task delegation should never be a casual dump like saying 'Please take care of this task!' as that steals the other person's time and destroys trust relationships; instead, follow careful, structured steps.

Step 1 of delegation: Select the appropriate person by checking whether they possess the necessary skills and knowledge for the task, whether it aligns with their personal growth aspirations and interests, and by understanding their current workload.

Step 2 of delegation: Share the background and purpose (the Why) before describing the actual work. Explain why the task is necessary, its significance, and its position in the bigger picture. Include a Q&A session to foster the other person's sense of initiative and ownership.

Example of sharing Why: 'I would like you to create this report because it will serve as important judgment material for next week's management meeting so that they can fully understand our team's contribution.'
Step 3 of delegation: Specifically define the expected results (the What) by clearly aligning on the Definition of Done rather than vague instructions like 'do it nicely.'

Definition of Done should cover: Output (e.g., 'a one-page A4 report using this format with three graphs inserted'), Quality level (e.g., 'a draft is fine so we can confirm the direction' versus 'client-ready quality that can be submitted as-is'), and Deadline (e.g., 'please let me review the first draft by Friday at 15:00').

Step 4 of delegation: Provide the necessary authority and resources (the How) by sharing access to required information and tools, the location of related materials, key people to consult, and any needed budget or tools, thereby creating an environment in which the person can actually complete the task.

Step 5 of task delegation (タスクの移譲): Agree in advance with the delegatee on the method and frequency of progress checks, including how much support will be provided and how much discretion they will have.

Example support rule for delegated work: If a problem causes work to stop for 30 minutes or more, the person should immediately speak up. This allows the delegatee to proceed with confidence while enabling the delegator to stay informed of the situation.
Step 6 of task delegation: After the work is completed, always review the deliverable and provide feedback. If it meets expectations, specifically praise what was good and express sincere gratitude.

When giving improvement feedback after delegation, do not blame the individual. Instead, adopt a collaborative process-review stance, such as saying 'Next time, doing it this way will make it even better.'
Task delegation not only frees up the delegator's time but also simultaneously increases the team's response capability and promotes the growth of team members.
A common practical barrier to delegation, even when the benefits are intellectually understood, is the belief that 'it is faster if I do it myself.'
If the sole purpose of delegation is to increase one's own free time (余白), it can trigger self-doubt about whether one is merely taking others' time and cognitive resources.

Shift perspective to the future when considering delegation: Even if you are currently the fastest at a task, consider whether the same situation is acceptable in 3 months. A team where only one person can perform the work versus a team with an additional capable person will have different overall speed.
Delegation is not a short-term optimization but an investment that increases the team's overall processing capacity.

Because delegation increases short-term load, start small rather than assigning large tasks immediately. Examples include handing over only part of a routine task or work up to the draft-creation stage, while agreeing on a higher frequency of check-ins at the beginning.

When deciding whom to delegate to, do not choose solely based on current strengths and weaknesses. Also consider whether the person is interested in the work and whether it overlaps with skills they want to develop, and consult the person themselves.
Delegation should be reframed not as imposing work on others but as a beneficial act for the entire team.
The small courage required to stop hoarding all work oneself is what lifts both the individual and the team to the next stage.

Large, vague tasks such as 'summarize a new feature proposal', 'develop a large-scale system', or 'create the second-half marketing strategy' often linger unfinished in task lists. Facing such huge tasks leads to hesitation about where to start, causing time to pass without progress and the day to end with nothing accomplished.

The human brain is wired to feel strong psychological resistance when the path to a goal is too long or the specific first step is unclear. This is known as procrastination (プロクラスティネーション), and the enormous size of a task is one of its primary triggers.

Oversized tasks also obstruct GTD (Getting Things Done) workflow. GTD's purpose is to move every 'thing that bothers you' out of your head into a trusted external system so you can focus lightly on 'what to do right now'. If a task remains at a coarse granularity like 'feature development', you cannot identify a concrete next action during the Process stage; reviewing the organized list merely overwhelms you and blocks the first step of Execute.

Most items captured in GTD as 'things that bother you' actually require multiple actions. GTD only functions once those items are broken down all the way to immediately executable, specific 'next actions'.

One practical approach is to decompose the work. When you freeze in front of a task it is usually because the next concrete step is ambiguous. Reverse-engineer from the final goal and list every necessary process—similar to building a WBS (Work Breakdown Structure).
Example of decomposition: Goal = 'publish a blog post'. First-level processes: planning, writing, review, publishing. Second-level breakdown of writing: write first draft, create figures, etc.

Tasks should be concretized to a level where both starting (着手) and completion (完了) can be clearly judged. This makes the immediate next step visible and renders the task more manageable both psychologically and practically.

For tasks whose overall picture is not yet clear, begin by asking 'What can I do first in order to get started?' rather than attempting to perfectly define the entire task before acting. Perfect definition as a prerequisite often becomes a burden that leads to procrastination.
Break the first action down to the smallest executable step that can be performed immediately in the current moment.

Example of starting small: For the task 'create proposal materials for a client,' do not begin by creating the materials themselves. Instead, take immediately doable first steps such as 'review last year’s proposal materials' or 'search for slides of past successful cases.' Once that step is finished, ask 'What is the next action?' and decide the subsequent concrete step. Chaining these next actions gradually reveals the outline of even an ambiguous task.

Tasks whose end point is inherently unclear (research, R&D, 'deepen understanding of X') tend to continue indefinitely because it is difficult to define 'how far is complete.' Time-boxing solves this by pairing a fixed time frame with a concrete deliverable.

Example of time-boxing: For the task 'understand the specifications of a legacy system through code reading,' it is hard to define rigorously what 'understood' means. Instead, set 'read for one week and, at that point, summarize the current understanding in slides.' The time-plus-deliverable combination creates a natural ending, makes the next required investigation visible, and turns open-ended learning into a progressing, completable task.
Task size guideline: Aim for tasks that can be completed in one day. Tasks that remain stuck in the 'in progress' column of a task board day after day are likely too large and should be split.
When splitting tasks, simply making them smaller is insufficient. Create 'good splits' so that your future self can take action without hesitation or confusion.

Condition for a good task split - Specificity: Use a clear subject and verb to describe a concrete action. Example: Instead of the vague 'research materials,' write 'Read Company A's latest press release and extract the main points as bullet points.' This allows anyone to visualize the exact same action.

Condition for a good task split - Clear completion: The split task must have objectively verifiable done/not-done criteria. Example: Instead of the ambiguous 'improve the design,' specify 'Change the button color on the website top page from red to blue,' which is immediately obvious when finished.
Condition for a good task split - Appropriate size: Keep each task no larger than what can reasonably be finished in a single day.

Ramen analogy for large tasks: Confronting a huge bowl of ramen can feel overwhelming, but breaking it into sequential parts—'first the vegetables, then the noodles, nibble some pork, dissolve garlic into the soup'—makes it finishable. Apply the same incremental approach to giant tasks.

Practical starting advice: Perfect decomposition is unnecessary. Begin by defining just the first small, concrete step. That initial action generates a strong sense of achievement and drives productivity gains.

Time is equally allocated as 24 hours per day to everyone, but outcomes and personal growth differ greatly depending on whether one passively allows time to be taken or actively designs and utilizes it.
Timeboxing and time blocking are methods for consciously designing one's schedule and taking control of time.
The 'Why now?' questioning technique combined with the Eisenhower Matrix helps determine task priorities effectively.
GTD (Getting Things Done) provides a systematic approach to task management.
Large tasks should be broken down into smaller parts and delegated where possible to improve manageability.

These time management techniques are not merely about efficiency; they restore control over time, enable results while creating buffer or margin (yohaku), prevent burnout, and expand future possibilities.
True time management means acting as the 'owner of time' by consciously controlling it rather than reacting to external demands.

After reclaiming time by eliminating 'time thieves' (such as excessive meetings and notifications), applying time blocking, and decomposing tasks, the focus shifts to how to productively use the protected time, for example empty 2-hour slots in a calendar or a 1-hour afternoon block created by disabling smartphone notifications.

Protected time must be actively utilized rather than filled with vague miscellaneous tasks, otherwise it becomes mere empty time; occasionally having unstructured 'do nothing' periods is valuable for rest, but the deliberate choice of activity—deep focused thinking, skill-building, or energy replenishment—determines whether time merely passes or becomes an investment that creates the future.
Absolute chronological time is identical for everyone (24 hours or 1440 minutes per day), yet the qualitative experience and outcomes of that time vary dramatically depending on how it is spent.
A casually executed hour of miscellaneous work has a fundamentally different meaning and impact compared with an hour spent pursuing a vividly imagined concrete goal such as 'I will finish this.'
Ancient Greek distinguishes two concepts of time: Chronos (クロノス), the quantitative, measurable time of clocks and calendars, and Kairos (カイロス), the qualitative, subjective, inner experience of time.

Kairos arises when a person becomes fully absorbed—e.g., a software engineer deep in coding or a designer lost in creation—producing a sensation of being detached from clock time and generating heightened creativity or sudden progress.
Kairos can also appear unexpectedly, such as when a stalled meeting discussion is unlocked by an apparently idle casual conversation that sparks a solution.
Kairos is therefore the non-measurable interval in which creativity surges and real advancement occurs, independent of Chronos.

Both terms are also names of Greek gods; Kairos is the god of opportunity, famously described by the proverb that 'chance has hair only in the front,' meaning opportunities must be seized immediately because they cannot be grasped once they have passed.
In ancient Greek, Chronos (クロノス) represents quantitative, measurable time that flows equally for everyone, while Kairos (カイロス) refers to qualitative time focused on the opportune moment or instant.

Most people instinctively think of time as Chronos when they hear the word 'time,' but the Greek distinction suggests that while quantitative time is given equally to all, how it is used is entirely up to the individual.
To truly utilize time means not merely consuming Chronos (letting hours pass) but perceiving time through Kairos and transforming it into 'time as opportunity.'

Even when the same amount of clock time elapses, productivity can vary dramatically: sometimes work progresses rapidly, other times concentration is lost and time is wasted. This variation is caused by natural waves of human energy and concentration.
The human body follows circadian rhythms driven by body temperature and hormone secretion cycles, producing repeating 'peaks' and 'valleys' of concentration and judgment ability throughout the day.
A typical circadian pattern for many people includes a concentration peak in the morning, a drop in attention after lunch, and a smaller secondary peak in the evening.
Understanding and aligning work with these personal energy waves (circadian rhythm) is a key method for converting Chronos into Kairos, i.e., turning ordinary time into high-opportunity moments.

Individual differences exist in daily productivity and concentration rhythms: some people are night types who become sharper and more productive as night approaches, while others are morning types who achieve their maximum productivity in the morning.
The key principle is to identify and understand 'during which time periods what kinds of work progress most effectively for oneself.'
The same one hour of time used during a period of high concentration becomes a 'meaningful investment,' but if used when tired it merely results in 'consumption.'
To effectively utilize time, it is essential to align with one's own biological/energy rhythm rather than strictly matching Chronos (clock time).

A practical method to determine one's energy-exertion timing is to observe natural wake-up time on holidays or long vacations with no constraints and without an alarm clock; this time is close to the body's inherent rhythm.
If a person naturally wakes at 6-7 AM or earlier even on days off and can be active from the morning onward, they are likely a morning type.

These ideas relate to the scientific concept of chronotypes, as discussed in research such as T. Roenneberg et al., 'Chronotype and Social Jetlag: A (Self-) Critical Review,' Biology, vol. 8, no. 3, p. 54, 2019.
A conceptual figure (2.18) illustrates differing concentration peak times across the day for morning types versus night types.

To identify if you are a night owl (夜型), observe holiday behavior: if mornings are spent groggy, you only crawl out of bed around noon, and you become more active toward evening, you may be night-oriented. Test this on days without accumulated fatigue, as busy weekdays can cause oversleeping from exhaustion.

Morning types (朝型) often wake naturally around 6-7 AM even on days off, despite wanting more sleep. They typically experience sharper mental performance and better productivity in the morning compared to evening hours. Evening events ending after 9 PM can feel particularly difficult.

Individual chronotypes vary widely even in similar environments. In one graduate lab example, a morning-type researcher worked from ~10 AM to 9 PM while most others arrived no earlier than 6 PM and some only after the morning person was leaving.

Track your personal concentration peaks by recording periods of high output (e.g., intense coding flow) versus low-energy periods. Over time this reveals patterns so you can protect high-focus blocks and avoid scheduling meetings during them.

Concentration is influenced not only by time of day but by preceding activities and context: light exercise or caffeine often boosts focus afterward; a large lunch commonly reduces it; anticipation of a major presentation or important meeting can make current work hard to start.

Focus conditions are highly individual. Traits such as post-meal sluggishness are not personal failings. Adapt scheduling to your own patterns rather than comparing yourself to others or forcing a universal routine.
Observing oneself reveals where Kairos (meaningful, qualitative time) appears within one's Chronos (quantitative, measurable time).
Time management should focus on the quality of time rather than its quantity; the next question is where to invest that high-quality time.

Prioritization techniques like the Eisenhower Matrix or GTD address how to organize existing tasks and decide 'what to do in this moment,' whereas this perspective asks 'what future value should limited time be invested in?'

Peter Drucker (The Effective Executive): 'There are always multiple things that ought to be done. But to produce results one must not spread oneself too thin. Concentration on one thing is necessary. If a change of pace is needed, two things may be done. But no one can do three or more things at the same time. Therefore, after considering what must be done, priorities must be set and kept.'
Although many tasks always present themselves, an individual can effectively handle only a limited number; attempting everything causes thoughts to scatter and results in accomplishing nothing.
The courage to choose what not to do is essential and constitutes the first step toward creating one's own future.
Everyone has exactly 24 hours in a day; whether that time is wasted or turned into an investment that connects to the future depends entirely on personal choice.
Time-allocation choices accumulate to shape career and life direction: for example, spending two hours on a formally opened regular meeting versus using that time to develop new ideas.
The essential principle is not to 'do everything' but to concentrate time on 'things that only you can do.'

Accepting every requested task one after another produces a certain sense of fulfillment ('I worked hard today and fulfilled everyone's expectations'), yet that fulfillment does not necessarily constitute an investment in the future and eventually turns into anxiety.
After recognizing the pattern, the author began consciously selecting which tasks to accept rather than taking on everything.
Utilizing time is not mere efficiency; it is the act of choosing where to invest for the future, and those successive choices largely determine one's career and life.
