Benefits of the 'Yes, if' approach: It provides additional information to the requester in a positive manner, allows you to accept only tasks within a feasible scope you feel capable of handling, and helps appropriately suppress personal stress.
Advice for handling feedback: Take a pause or 'one breath' (一呼吸置く) before responding to feedback, especially negative comments.

Historical evolution of code reviews: In the past, code reviews involved printing completed source code on paper for a superior to check and approve, functioning as a somewhat ritualistic process. This has evolved into pull request (PR) reviews, which is a positive change for improving code quality and design quality.
Communication challenges in modern code reviews: Review comments can evoke negative emotions, such as feeling that a certain writing style is unacceptable.

Examples of overly negative or unhelpful code review comments to avoid: 'This writing style is impossible' (この書き方はありえない), 'The design is too dirty' (設計が汚すぎる), 'Please rewrite everything' (全部書き直してほしい).

In code reviews, writing comments that personally attack individuals is inappropriate. Teams should establish working agreements (ワーキングアグリーメント) that prohibit disrespectful writing so that such behavior can be called out if it occurs.

Even polite and well-written review comments can still trigger negative emotions such as feeling that the feedback is overly detailed or unnecessary. If a flash of irritation or anger arises and one is tempted to ignore the comment, pause immediately, take a deep breath, and reread the comment slowly and carefully.

Evaluate review feedback by asking whether incorporating it will make the current code or design better. If the answer is yes, accept and apply the feedback. If one still prefers not to incorporate it, initiate a direct conversation with the reviewer rather than reacting emotionally.
Direct dialogue about review comments is essential because it helps raise the quality of code developed by the team.
When anger arises during a review, take a single breath to regain composure. Calming down makes the appropriate next action become clear.

Major changes such as stopping a development effort due to a business pivot or handing over tasks because of organizational restructuring can feel like wasted effort. These moments are actually opportunities to convert personal experience into reusable assets.

To turn experience into a reusable asset, write down what was achieved, what regrets remain, what decisions were made, and what conflicts or trade-offs were involved. This process converts tacit knowledge (暗黙知) into explicit, reusable knowledge.

The author personally experienced the sudden dissolution of an entire department at the end of their second year as a new graduate due to the Lehman Shock, which required abandoning ongoing development work; documenting such events turns them into lasting professional assets.

When leaving a project or handing over work, complete unfinished items and thoroughly document processes (such as batch file usage and testing procedures) so that the incoming team can continue without confusion or blockers.

The act of documenting work for handover forces explicit language around implicit knowledge; this process itself deepens the original author's own understanding of practices such as testing methodology.
Completing work thoroughly (やりきること) is an intangible but highly valuable professional asset that remains even after you leave a role or project.

Past efforts and experiences are never wasted; they become supporting components of your professional identity and future capability. When you must leave unfinished work, convert the experience into an asset rather than dwelling on loss.

Engineers should communicate with data rather than emotion when advocating for change. Feelings of frustration about technical debt or rejected tool requests are natural, but data turns complaints into actionable improvement proposals.

Useful metrics for arguing technical-debt repayment or process improvement include: cyclomatic complexity (循環的複雑度), change frequency (変更頻度), bug occurrence rate (バグ発生率), and cycle-time changes from personal experiments.

A data-backed proposal is more effective than a vague request. Example transformation: instead of 'I want to repay technical debt,' say 'Over the past three months the bug occurrence rate has risen 50 % and the amount of code whose cyclomatic complexity exceeds 30 has increased. Shall we allocate time to refactoring in order to reduce complexity and therefore bugs?'

When both the current problem and the expected benefit of solving it are made concrete and quantified, the proposal becomes comparable to other competing tasks and therefore easier for decision-makers to evaluate and approve.

Personal experiments (e.g., measuring cycle-time improvement after trying a new tool yourself) and external success stories can serve as supporting evidence when requesting organizational adoption of productivity tools.

Before listening to others (e.g., in 1-on-1s), first check and prepare your own capacity to listen. If you are fatigued, distracted by pending tasks, or mentally elsewhere, you are not in a state to truly hear someone.

Managers should have the courage to reschedule conversations when not in good condition, saying something like: 'Sorry, I'm not in good condition today, please let me reschedule.' This allows for genuine dialogue later rather than a hollow meeting.

Rigid 'should' thinking (e.g., 'managers must always do 1-on-1s frequently') can exhaust a manager. It is better to operate within one's actual capability than to attend meetings in a mentally absent state.
Managers should face their own capability honestly and adjust their workload to a sustainable, 'life-size' range, using task and time management techniques.
When conflicts arise in a team, look at the structure rather than the people. Interpersonal clashes generate stress for both the team and the manager who must deal with them.
Instead of confronting the stress of conflict head-on, a manager should investigate why the conflict occurred in the first place (focusing on underlying structure or systems).

When opinions conflict, focus on the underlying structure rather than the people: examine the background behind person A's 'this is how it should be,' including the merits and demerits of following that view, and identify the specific situations where person B's version of correctness applies versus when it does not.

ABC theory is effective for resolving clashes over the same event: conflicting opinions stem from gaps in background and values; trace each person's values, capture the landscape as they see it, then calmly determine how the group should act.
Shifting attention from people (hito) to matters (koto) and then to structure transforms emotional confrontations into constructive material for problem-solving.

The most important tip for managers is to regularly inventory one's own emotions; remaining unaware of personal feelings or deprioritizing self-care leads to unnoticed exhaustion and eventual burnout.

Practical methods for self-awareness include periodically recording emotions (e.g., daily self-questioning 'Am I energetic today or not?' or weekend lists of 'things that were tough this week') and using digital tools such as smartwatch health apps.

The author uses a Fitbit device to track a stress-management score derived from heart rate, sleep duration, and other physiological data; a declining score prompts slowing the activity pace as a behavioral change.
A manager being in a good mood (gokigen) is a prerequisite condition for the team being in a good mood; therefore self-care must not be neglected.
Burnout syndrome (燃え尽き症候群) is characterized by a sense of complete exhaustion, inability to feel passion for one's work, and loss of self-confidence.

Completely avoiding burnout from the outset can be difficult in work or life styles that involve jumping into high-uncertainty situations; therefore, one should acknowledge the risk and focus on detecting early warning signs.

Personal early signs of approaching burnout (author's experience): constantly thinking about work even during free time, but experiencing a sense of confinement/obstruction rather than excitement or thrill.

Additional burnout signs: decreased energy and vitality for hobby or leisure activities; ending the day with a persistent feeling of having accomplished nothing; craving extremely spicy food yet barely tasting the spiciness.
Inability to think of content for a daily work report (日報) can serve as a concrete, observable warning signal of impending burnout.

Remote-work environments make declining vitality harder to notice because one can continue working without the physical cue of 'I don't want to go to the office'; therefore, individuals must deliberately identify and monitor their own personal signals.
Burnout situations can arise repeatedly and unexpectedly, even after previous episodes, underscoring the need for ongoing self-monitoring rather than one-time prevention.
To prevent burnout, first acknowledge that you are burning out or losing vitality: recognize 'I am starting to burn out, I am losing energy.'

If possible, rest when burning out. However, if work remains on your mind even during rest, confront those lingering concerns and address them within the work itself (noted as a relatively 'macho' approach; fully resting is often better).
When burning out, deliberately cut off work-related activities even on holidays (such as reading or using a PC for work-related tasks) to gradually reduce the time the brain is linked to work.

When not feeling well or burning out, keep alcohol at a distance. While 1-2 drinks may be acceptable, drinking more when feeling down provides only momentary pleasure followed by a sense of emptiness or lethargy.
Consulting someone and sharing the suffering can be an excellent method to resolve burnout, as gaining empathy can lighten the heart.
Burnout occurs when mind-share is completely taken over by something; therefore, taking actions that create space or margin in one's mind-share is important to prevent burnout.
Recovery from near-burnout is not immediate even after taking preventive actions; it takes 1-2 weeks or more of slowly creating mental space before faded passion resurfaces.

Burnout can occur not only in work but also in hobbies, especially those requiring skill (like playing an instrument) when things aren't going well or become tangled; in such cases, one option is to deliberately set the hobby aside for a while and create distance.
Complete burnout makes recovery very difficult, so it is important to regularly face oneself and initiate recovery at a moderate stage before reaching full burnout.
ソフトウェアエンジニアは学び続けることを宿命づけられた存在であり、特にこの業界では学び続けることの重要性が強調されている。
環境の変化が非常に速く、学び続ける姿勢なしにはスキル・ナレッジがあっという間に陳腐化してしまうという特性がある。
変化は主に3点で起こっている（技術進化のサイクル、市場・顧客要求のトレンド、およびページ上で明示されていない第3点）。
技術進化のサイクル：2000年代以降に絞っても、クラウド、マイクロサービス、コンテナ、サーバーレス、AI／機械学習、ローコード・ノーコードなど新しい技術が目まぐるしく登場している。2025年現在ではLLM・Coding Agentが隆盛を極め、さらに進化のサイクルが加速している。
2001年のアジャイルソフトウェア開発宣言の「アジャイル宣言の背後にある原則」には「動くソフトウェアを、2～3週間から2～3か月というできるだけ短い時間間隔でリリースします」という記述がある。
アジャイル開発、DevOpsが浸透していく中で、2～3週間どころか一日に何回もデプロイするような状況さえある。
市場・顧客要求のトレンド：多くのソフトウェアは一度つくったら終わりではなく、リリース後でも顧客要望に応えて改良し続けることが求められている。
販売チャネル自体がPC、フィーチャーフォン、スマートフォン、タブレット、スマートウォッチなど変化・多様化している。
特にスマートフォン・タブレット・スマートウォッチは端末自体が高頻度にOSを更新していくため、必然的にソフトウェアも変化を求められる。

In the software industry, the speed of competition and selection is high: emerging companies can rapidly transform markets using technology as a weapon, making it difficult even for top companies to maintain their position for long. This is why continuous learning is essential.

Being in the software industry naturally provides opportunities to encounter new things, so one will learn even if left alone. However, there is a large difference in growth speed and ultimate achievement level between learning as a result of being swept along by surrounding changes versus taking the initiative and learning proactively with a sense of ownership.
Skill Management (スキルマネジメント) refers not only to maintaining and acquiring skills, but also to cultivating and organizing the very attitude of continuing to learn.
When first jumping into a role as an engineer or manager, one does not know the ropes and experiences various failures. People grow by overcoming those failures.
A sign of having properly honed skills over a career is looking back at code written in one's first year after several years have passed and feeling that it is immature and embarrassing.

In a long career, there are moments of feeling stuck or stagnant. This arrives as anxiety such as 'Is this okay as it is?', causing inner unrest. One may be producing results yet feel unfulfilled, or be putting in effort yet feel that the heart is not keeping up.
Growth is not a straight rightward-upward line. It is a process of sometimes repeating stagnation or setbacks while gradually climbing to higher levels.
Even when producing results, one may not feel a sense of accomplishment or satisfaction. Even when stacking up effort, one may not feel the same sense of growth as before.
プラトー状態（高原状態） is a temporary stagnation in the progress of learning or work, characterized by periods where results are hard to see and there is no sense of accomplishment or feedback.
Growth is not linear: many people imagine growth as a straight upward line, but the actual growth curve includes plateaus (stagnation periods) after initial progress.
Plateaus visit everyone; remaining stuck in a plateau versus overcoming it to achieve further growth is a matter of personal choice and attitude.
Long-term continuous growth through the ups and downs of learning requires a specific 'attitude toward growth' (成長に向き合う姿勢).

People who keep growing do not leave things to the environment or wait for a superior's instructions; they proactively initiate change by asking 'What can I do right now?' and 'How can I make use of this situation?'

Example of proactive change: When a project offers exposure to new technology, do not draw a boundary saying 'this is outside my job scope'; instead, investigate it with genuine interest. Such small attempts broaden the range of experience and eventually connect to major growth.

According to Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP), learning consists of 5 stages, beginning with 'unconscious incompetence' (無意識的無能: 知らないしできない — you don't know it and can't do it) and progressing through higher levels of awareness and skill.

The 5 stages of learning (学習の5段階) are: 1. Unconscious incompetence (無意識的無能: don't know and can't do); 2. Conscious incompetence (意識的無能: know it but still can't do it); 3. Conscious competence (意識的有能: can do it if you think about it); 4. Unconscious competence (無意識的有能: can do it without thinking); 5. Unconscious competence made conscious (無意識的有能に意識的有能: can teach it from anywhere / explain it to others).
When people actively jump into change or new challenges, they commonly experience the feeling that 'it's not going well' because they start at the unconscious incompetence stage.

Even after overcoming initial difficulty and making smooth progress, learners often encounter a plateau (プラトー現象) where growth stalls: 'It was going reasonably well at first, but gradually it stops going well.'

The plateau occurs precisely because learning has expanded the known area, which in turn makes previously invisible 'unknowns' become visible: as learning advances, more of what you don't know comes into view.
NLP originated in therapy and counseling settings and is applied across medicine, business, education, family, and childcare.

Learning begins with vague expectations ('I want to learn X'), often followed by an initial phase of unexpected understanding and a feeling of 'I can do this,' creating early-stage momentum and a sense of accomplishment.
A common later barrier is knowing something intellectually but being unable to reproduce or apply it in real situations; the difficulty lies in converting understanding into action.

The five stages of learning help explain this barrier: moving from 'know but cannot do' to 'can do if I think about it' requires deepening understanding and reorganizing knowledge internally, not merely accumulating more facts.
Moving from 'can do if I think' to 'can do without thinking' requires repeated practice that converts knowledge into bodily/tacit knowledge (身体知), so that action becomes automatic.
Each advance to the next stage demands acquiring the capabilities of the higher level, creating a skill gap; inability to close the gap causes confidence to fluctuate.
The Dunning-Kruger effect illustrates these confidence fluctuations during skill acquisition, relating self-evaluation to the amount of experience or learning (shown conceptually in Figure 4.3).
A core insight of the page is that learning itself increases awareness of what one does not know.

The Dunning-Kruger effect is a cognitive bias in which people with insufficient experience or skill in a domain find it harder to accurately estimate their own understanding or performance, and therefore tend to overestimate themselves; judging quality in that domain itself requires knowledge and skill.

Beginner programmers typically start from a superficial understanding ('programming lets you make software'). After following tutorials and getting short scripts or simple apps to run without errors, they often conclude that programming is surprisingly easy, because the overall difficulty and pitfalls are not yet visible.

When they attempt more demanding requirements (persisting data, navigating between screens, making something usable by others), errors appear and previously unnoticed concepts surface—variable scope, asynchronous processing, exception handling, security—revealing that they knew only a tiny fragment of the domain.
Further learning makes the extent of unknown territory more visible, causing self-evaluation to become unstable; many people lose confidence and even conclude they are unsuited to the field.

This dip in confidence is a sign that learning has entered a new stage. Analogous to an athlete whose scores temporarily drop while correcting form, old patterns must be broken, producing short-term performance fluctuation.
Accepting that instability and continuing trial-and-error plus feedback gradually enables a person to distinguish what they know from what they do not know.
Modern high-quality AI coding assistants (e.g., Claude Code) can delay or reduce encounters with walls, thereby decreasing opportunities to notice the existence of unknown regions.
As experience accumulates and learning is applied in professional practice, new unknowns continually appear; writing working programs is no longer sufficient.
Professional software work additionally requires writing readable code, building team-maintainable systems, and designing operations that avoid failures.
Essential complementary capabilities include design philosophy, review culture, test automation, documentation, and communication skills.

Through such experience self-evaluation gradually converges on reality: one adopts the premise that one's own understanding remains limited, thinks more carefully, and listens to others, thereby advancing learning.
Continuous change and lifelong learning necessarily enlarge the set of things one does not know; this expansion should not be feared.
The Dunning-Kruger effect predicts that once a person believes they have grasped a domain to a reasonable degree, further progress reveals many remaining unknowns and inabilities.
The learner therefore moves from the state of 'not knowing that one does not know' (ignorance of ignorance) to the state of 'knowing that one does not know' (knowledge of ignorance).
Deepening comprehension of any subject expands the region of perceived unknowns (illustrated by Figure 4.4).

Jumping into a new field or role (e.g., an engineer becoming a manager) presents an entirely different landscape of challenges such as team building, task management, external coordination, long-term strategy, and stakeholder management; initial incompetence and setbacks are inevitable, yet one must persist and move forward.
Countless childhood failures leave lingering bitter memories that unconsciously slow people down and make them hesitate to take on new challenges as adults.

People who keep growing and changing deliberately jump into situations that make their feet freeze; they intentionally place themselves where they are the least skilled person present, thereby creating environments that consist only of growth potential (referenced from Chad Fowler's The Passionate Programmer).

Intellectual humility (知的な謙虚さ) is the stance of remaining open to others' opinions and new information because one starts from the premise 'there are still things I do not know.' This attitude enables learning from anyone regardless of age or rank.

People whose growth stops typically suffer from complacency ('I already know enough') or from an aversion to the failures that accompany learning something new; they therefore close their ears to new information.
Those who possess intellectual humility have the flexibility to absorb other people's wisdom as their own learning.

In a team, the courage to say 'I don't know' generates trust. Teams that can frankly share what they do not understand cultivate a culture of mutual learning, accelerate everyone's growth, and thereby create the very soil of psychological safety.
An individual's humble, learning-oriented attitude produces positive effects not only for that person but for the entire group or organization to which they belong.
Intellectual humility in professional settings can be demonstrated through specific behaviors that prioritize curiosity and learning over defensiveness.

In code reviews, when encountering a differing opinion, intellectually humble behavior involves first accepting the input without immediate rebuttal and asking questions such as 'I want to know what benefits there are to taking that approach!' to understand the rationale.
In pair programming, if a partner uses an unfamiliar shortcut key or command, an intellectually humble response is to honestly ask 'How do you do that?' rather than pretending to know.
In meetings, when encountering an unknown technical term, intellectually humble behavior includes having the courage to speak up and say 'Sorry, please teach me the meaning of that word.'
Continuous learners consciously seek out learning environments such as seminars, training sessions, and technical communities where highly motivated people gather.
Technical communities provide not only systematized knowledge but also living, practical information and high levels of enthusiasm that formal settings may lack.
Learning events have become more accessible regardless of location due to the growth of local communities and the increase in online and hybrid formats.
Participation in learning communities serves dual purposes: receiving information and connecting with like-minded peers to discuss ideas, relativize one's own thinking, and gain new perspectives.
Modern learners have abundant input sources including books, web articles, podcasts, and videos, many of which are systematically organized or designed specifically to aid understanding.
A recommended approach for learning an unfamiliar field is to start with introductory books and then follow the citations and references within those books to deepen knowledge.
A common learning approach is to use small pockets of time or holidays for consistent, incremental input to deepen understanding.

Output-based learning (e.g., writing blog posts or presenting at tech events) is an excellent method: it organizes and systematizes tacit knowledge (implicit, unverbalized knowledge and experience) into explicit knowledge that can be shared with others. This process clarifies what one understands versus what is lacking, revealing the next learning direction and leading to deeper, more robust learning.

Learning opportunities exist in daily life, such as observing a colleague's shortcut key usage during mob programming or overhearing another team's initiatives. Capture these small insights immediately via notes or brief Slack posts so they become internalized rather than fleeting.

The key to integrating learning into daily life is not expecting 'perfect learning time.' Even 10 minutes on a commute or 5 minutes before a meeting suffice. Small accumulations eventually connect: 'dots become lines, and lines become surfaces.' Growth is the process where accumulated points suddenly gain meaning and connect.

Reflection (内省/リフレクション) means reviewing one's experiences, assigning meaning to them, and applying insights going forward. It is not mere self-criticism but verbalizing and weaving together one's experiences.

Narrativization (物語化) of events: Retelling occurrences as a story transforms a mere failure anecdote into a framework for overviewing how it connected to learning. This enables objective viewing and reinterpretation as one's own growth narrative.

Narratives for learning do not require novel-length writing. Even bullet points or messy notes answering 'What did I know at the time?', 'What did I realize I did not know?', and 'How did I feel?' will shape your personal learning storyline.

Habitual reflection (習慣的なふりかえり) is one of the most important processes in learning. By assigning meaning to inputted knowledge and experienced events and internalizing them, knowledge and experience are sublimated into living wisdom (血肉の通った知恵).

The term ふりかえり encompasses both retrospective (レトロスペクティブ: focusing on what actually happened and subsequent improvements) and reflection (リフレクション: putting inner discoveries into words). The discussion here addresses the latter—personal reflection.

Multi-angle reflection prompts for capturing learning: What did I newly learn? How does it connect with previous knowledge? What was unexpected? What felt easy to do? What felt difficult? If I were to change something starting tomorrow, what would I do?
Daily self-questioning connects fragmented information with one's existing knowledge and experience.
The ability to pose good questions is honed by consciously asking them during daily reflections.
Helpful habit: pose questions such as 'How should I think to see alternative options?' or 'Why did I feel that way?' to oneself or others.

David Kolb (organizational behavior scholar) proposed the Experiential Learning Model, which theorizes the process of learning from experience (Kolb, D. A., 1984, Experiential Learning: Experience as the Source of Learning and Development).
Kolb's Experiential Learning Model cycle consists of four stages: 実践 (Active Experimentation/Practice), 経験 (Concrete Experience), 概念化 (Abstract Conceptualization), and 省察 (Reflective Observation).

Example of applying the model: When a system under development crashes in the production environment, the top priority is to restore it as quickly as possible, but the incident is also an excellent learning opportunity.

The experiential learning/reflection cycle consists of four stages: 経験 (Experience: encountering a situation), 省察 (Reflection: examining why it happened and why it wasn't caught earlier), 概念化 (Conceptualization: forming a general principle or lesson), and 実践 (Practice: applying the lesson more broadly and verifying it).

Concrete example of the cycle applied to a production software failure: Experience involved a reported system crash from a specific operation; logs revealed a NullPointerException that was then fixed. Reflection asked why the bug occurred, why tests missed it, and why it did not appear in the verification environment. Conceptualization concluded that an external API expected always to return an object can actually return Null, and because external API behavior cannot be fully controlled, Null checks and type checks must always be performed. Practice added the Null checks, created tests that force a Null return to confirm proper error handling, and applied the same pattern to every location that uses external APIs.

Failures are especially valuable learning opportunities: “失敗だからこそ大きな学びが得られる” (precisely because it is a failure, large learning can be obtained). People who keep practicing reflection convert their experiences into “再利用可能な資産” (reusable assets).

Growth plateaus produce the feeling “I am working harder than before yet getting no results.” This is not a decline in ability but a signal that the current methods can no longer overcome the next stage.

Unsuccessful periods tempt people to focus only on “what I could not do,” which, when prolonged, leads to demotivation or resignation (“maybe I just cannot do it”). The correct stance is to observe carefully why the outcome occurred rather than blaming the failure itself.
The purpose of reflection is never to judge the past but to discover hints for moving forward: “ふりかえりの目的は、過去を裁くことではなく、次に進むためのヒントを見つけること.”

When experiencing negative emotions in a period of stagnation, do not look away from them or detach; instead, record the feelings as they are without analyzing them (e.g., '悔しい' / frustrated, '焦っていた' / was impatient, '周囲の期待を気にしていた' / was concerned about others' expectations). Recording emotions this way enables distinguishing facts from emotions, serving as the first step toward calmly considering the next action.

Shift focus from things that could not be done to things that were tried. During plateaus, the mind often fills with a 'failure list'; instead, write down what experiments were attempted. Even unsuccessful challenges are valuable experimental results. Reflecting on the hypotheses formed and the conditions under which they were tested reveals how to act next.

Even when progress appears stagnant, change is always present. Examples include becoming able to identify the causes of failure more quickly than before, or having an increased number of people available for consultation. The ability to notice these small changes generates the energy needed to face forward again.

Focus on change rather than results (成果ではなく変化に着目する). While outcomes matter, new challenges often fail to produce immediate results; the key is to notice what has changed compared with yesterday's self rather than dwelling on the absence of results.

Do not overlook small changes, which are hidden throughout daily life and work. Example: previously leaving an entire repository to other team members, but now being able to add even a single comment on a pull request; or generating the intended code in a single attempt.

Small personal improvements (such as writing better prompts or receiving more blog views) quickly become ordinary, so people often fail to notice that something they could not do yesterday is now possible today.
Deliberately noticing these small differences and treating them as evidence of growth cultivates self-efficacy.
Regular retrospectives and brief daily notes serve as practical tools for detecting one's own incremental changes.
The ability to detect change is equivalent to the ability to generate one's own motivation (self-supplied motivation) rather than depending on external evaluation.
By assigning meaning to even tiny shifts, an individual can turn those shifts into a continuous source of growth energy.

Large-scale outcomes may be delayed, yet smaller units of work almost always contain recognizable micro-achievements; examples include a single feature that now functions, newly written test code that will verify future implementations, or the simple act of scheduling regular 1-on-1 meetings that prepare the ground for developmental conversations.
Progressing from one micro-achievement to the next via baby steps converts the experience of change itself into sustained motivation.
A complementary method for visualizing change is to keep explicit records of one's past self, documenting with the conscious purpose of capturing differences over time.

Daily growth-tracking questions to record consistently: What did I do today? What new thing did I try today? What new thing can I now do? Why was I able to do it? Accumulating these small daily records allows later reflection (e.g., after six months) to reveal that previously struggled-with tasks have become ordinary, showing that growth includes the ability to recognize change.

Those who can enjoy change are the ones who grow. The common trait of people who keep growing is not special talent or a privileged environment, but an attitude of not fearing change, reflecting on oneself, and making learning a daily habit.

Change is frightening for everyone, but starting with small steps eases anxiety. Begin with nearby learning opportunities rather than sudden large challenges. Self-growth through learning has no finish line; after pausing to acknowledge progress, new paths appear. The present is shaped by daily choices and accumulated learning, so one should enjoy change and keep growing.

The path of learning and mastery is never flat, analogous to seasons: spring-like new beginnings (sprouting), plateaus, and winter-like periods of steady, unglamorous experience accumulation. People often treat only smooth, spring-like progress as correct and thus feel impatient during stagnation, yet every learning phase has meaning just as every season does.

Continue at one's own pace while holding a personal compass; each step becomes nourishment that elevates skills. This content appears in a skill-management framework discussing the common points of people who continue to grow.

Even when one decides to continuously grow and develop oneself, actually taking action is not easy; common obstacles include inability to concentrate when opening a book, prioritizing immediate work when trying to make time, and falling into the habit of saying 'I'll do it tomorrow.'

People oscillate between the desire to grow and real-world constraints; failing to follow through can lead to labeling oneself as lazy and falling into self-loathing, but this is neither laziness nor weakness of will—it is a structural wall.

These structural walls consist of two types of forces: exogenous (external) forces such as workplace systems and culture, and endogenous (internal) forces such as psychological, emotional, and thinking patterns.
The first step to continuing to grow is to understand the existence of these two types of walls (exogenous and endogenous).

The 'walls' discussed are not meant to point out an individual's lack of effort; they are a framework for visualizing the 'unconsciously operating forces' within the environments and cultures we belong to.
Understanding these walls is not about taking on responsibility, but rather the first step toward redesigning the relationship between one's environment and oneself.

Exogenous walls created by the surrounding environment are difficult to move through personal will or effort alone, but knowing what walls exist allows one to understand in advance how to confront them.

The 'busyness wall' (忙しさの壁) is an exogenous constraint: one plans to allocate time for input/learning, but the day fills with Slack notifications, meetings, and review responses; intending to study after work, one is too exhausted from daytime busyness to engage in input.
Many people feel they lack time and postpone new challenges with phrases like 'I know it's important, but I just don't have the time.'

The real issue is often not a shortage of time but unclear priorities. If asking yourself 'How much time would I actually need to work on this?' leaves you stuck for an answer, you are likely trapped in a situation where priorities have become invisible.

In daily work, high-urgency items (requests from others, messages demanding immediate replies, and immediate defects) tend to be assigned high priority, while non-urgent items—even important ones—are postponed with the thought 'If it doesn't have to be done right now, it can wait.'

The Eisenhower Matrix (introduced in Chapter 2) classifies tasks by importance and urgency into four quadrants: Quadrant 1 (important and urgent), Quadrant 2 (important but not urgent), Quadrant 3 (not important but urgent), and Quadrant 4 (neither important nor urgent).
Quadrant 2 tasks ('important but not urgent') are those that lead to future results and personal growth; they must not be postponed and require conscious time allocation.
High-urgency quadrants (1 and 3) are naturally prioritized, while low-urgency quadrants (2 and 4) tend to be deprioritized, which systematically hinders self-development.
Important Quadrant II tasks (important but not urgent) that drive future results and growth often remain untouched because urgent Quadrant I and Quadrant III tasks are prioritized instead.

Neglecting self-development time creates a vicious cycle: no time allocated to skill-building → the only way to improve at handling current tasks is through on-the-job practice → work efficiency improves only slowly.
Regularly scheduled meetings can consume the time needed for self-improvement; without monitoring how much of the workday meetings occupy, it is easy to end up with half the day spent in meetings.
When meetings dominate the day, remaining energy after work hours is depleted, making it even harder to secure time for self-study.

Engineer example of interrupt-driven work: while studying a new library, a Slack request arrives demanding a same-day fix; while refactoring, consecutive review requests arrive and break concentration.
Engineer example of meeting fragmentation: morning filled by recurring meetings plus sudden afternoon meetings leave no contiguous block of focused time.

Manager example of consultation load: desire to craft a new technical strategy is displaced by a full day of technical pair-programming, career counseling, and interpersonal mediation; simultaneous Slack DMs force repeated context-switching that exhausts energy.

Manager example of hiring/evaluation overload: long-term roadmap thinking is displaced by document screening, interviews, and offer meetings; evaluation season fills the calendar with 1-on-1s and calibration meetings, postponing other work.

Manager example of cross-department coordination: sudden spec-change discussions and progress-report preparation consume time that could have been spent on organizational issues; data aggregation and slide creation for executive meetings further erode available hours.

The root of busyness lies in an implicit success equation that 'the more you do, the more your value is proven.' Japanese workplace culture strongly equates high utilization rates with 'working hard,' treating time for contemplation and reflection as low-productivity behavior, which systematically steals time for learning.

Busyness itself is a numbing sensation: temporary overload can be perceived as discomfort, but chronic busyness causes the discomfort to fade so that the state feels normal. This makes busyness an unrecognized wall that must first be made visible.

To break through the busyness wall, begin by visualizing it: review the day's planned schedule at the start, then at the end of the day reflect on and record all work actually performed (including unplanned tasks). The accumulated record creates awareness.
A recommended next step is to protect learning time by treating it as a 'second domain' and scheduling it first. Even 30 minutes once a week blocked on the calendar is sufficient to start.

The information-overload wall arises because the moment one wants to learn, infinite materials (books, web articles, podcasts, videos, seminars) become instantly available, making it difficult to discern which information is actually needed.
Humans respond positively to a moderate number of choices, but an excessive number produces anxiety or decision paralysis that prevents action.

The classic jam experiment (Iyengar & Lepper, 2000) demonstrated this: a display of 24 jam varieties produced more tasting but only a 3 % purchase rate, whereas a display of 6 varieties produced fewer tastings yet a substantially higher purchase rate.

A classic choice experiment (implied jam study) showed that more options attract interest but reduce actual decisions: purchase rate reached 30% with fewer choices, creating a large gap versus abundant options.

Abundant choices provide freedom but trigger a brain stress response called '決定回避' (decision avoidance). Intellectual workers especially expend energy on judging which information to select, leading to burnout before taking action.
Information overload appears in practice as '調べすぎて結論が出ない' (over-researching without reaching a conclusion) and '情報の深追いが目的化する' (chasing deeper information becoming an end in itself).
Recommended countermeasures: deliberately limit information sources, impose time cutoffs on research then switch to action, and systematically narrow the set of choices.
Self-development is a social act, not purely individual will. Continuation of challenges depends heavily on whether supportive people exist and whether the environment tolerates failure.

Absence of psychologically safe relationships in which one can display immaturity produces defensive behavior: the feeling that work cannot be shown until it is 'perfect' often signals underlying relational anxiety.

Online-centric workplaces reduce non-verbal encouragement and incidental observation of others' efforts. Casual office visibility of a colleague's trial-and-error once served as an implicit stimulus ('I should try too'); its loss lowers the visibility of others' learning and increases isolation.

Learning stagnation is frequently caused by missing social support rather than low personal motivation. A single remark such as 'isn't that inefficient?' from a colleague can extinguish the will to retry by amplifying fear of exposing incompleteness.

A key barrier to autonomous learning is the confusion between 'support' (支援) and 'interference' (干渉). Even well-intentioned bosses or mentors frequently issue detailed instructions and advice, which recipients experience as being watched or pressured to meet expectations. This erodes the 'space to design one's own learning' (自分の学びを自分でデザインする余白) and undermines learning autonomy through a misunderstanding of what genuine support looks like.

An effective way to address support-interference confusion is to designate a single consultation partner and explicitly verbalize the desired form of support. Concrete examples include: 'I just want you to confirm the direction,' 'Please check whether my understanding so far is correct,' or 'Tell me only one improvement point.' Repeated exchanges of this type build a sense of psychological safety, making it acceptable to expose immaturity and enabling confident challenge-taking.

Internal (endogenous) barriers arise from the mind's 'defense reaction to change' (変化への防衛反応). Because the barrier is self-generated it can trigger self-loathing ('I am lazy'), yet it is neither malice nor laziness; it is a self-protective mechanism (自分を守る仕組み).

The human brain is wired to maintain the status quo. Prospect Theory (プロスペクト理論), proposed by Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky, includes the principle of loss aversion (損失回避): people preferentially avoid possible losses over possible gains from change. When options are numerous or the impact of change is uncertain, individuals default to the psychologically safer choice of inaction and status-quo preservation.
Resistance to change manifests in two principal forms within self-development contexts (specific forms not detailed on this page).

Two main forms of resistance to adopting new tools or methods: (1) 'status quo maintenance' — not even trying because the current way already feels convenient enough; (2) 'failure of unlearning' — having tried something new but being unable to let go of the old approach.

Long success in the same work makes people believe 'my way is correct' or 'this is the only way,' leading them to empathize with confirming information and ignore or downplay contradictory information (confirmation bias).

Code-review example of unlearning failure: seeing another member's approach and thinking 'theoretically that design might be valid, but my way is absolutely better,' then pushing one's own claim instead of learning the new idea, thereby missing the learning opportunity.

The tendency to cling to proven patterns is stronger among people with long success histories, especially mid-level and managerial staff who feel they must 'protect their area of expertise,' which blocks learning in new domains. Greater experience increases dependence on one's 'favorite patterns' — an almost inevitable phenomenon for high-achievers.

Resistance to change is not inherently bad; it is a brain defense mechanism that avoids perceived danger. The problem arises when the defense over-activates and repeatedly stops a person at the entrance to learning or midway through re-learning.

Breaking the status quo need not be dramatic: even reading one blog post, trying a new tool in a personal environment, or incorporating a newly learned design technique into a small pull request constitutes a change. Consciously repeating such small steps is recommended.

Emotional barrier: observing people who are far ahead in the same self-improvement domain can serve as motivational fuel ('I want to become like that') or generate negative emotions and anxiety ('I'll never be like them,' 'I'm already behind').
Modern SNS floods people with information about countless unrelated others, making unconscious social comparison almost automatic and amplifying both inspiration and self-doubt.

Seeing more advanced people can trigger perfectionist thoughts such as 'I must be like that,' which then leads to stopping action with the belief that 'it's better not to do it at all than to do it halfway.'
The strongest emotional deterrent to self-development is shame, which arises from the anticipation that one might be seen by others as insufficient or inadequate.
A single memory in an organization that 'showing immaturity lowers evaluation' is enough to make people avoid challenges based solely on that anticipation.

Shame is linked to specific past experiences such as reprimand, being looked down upon, or comparison, and therefore cannot be overcome by logic or reasoning; it becomes the largest emotional wall blocking self-development.
Fear is a reaction for avoiding danger, whereas shame is a reaction for maintaining relationships with others; at the root of shame lies the pain that 'the relationship might break.'
Fearing failure in a learning environment is therefore a natural response.

The key is not to deny these emotions but to observe them; emotional and thought patterns are not defects but natural survival mechanisms, and understanding them enables more flexible living rather than self-blame.
A second fundamental wall that stalls self-development is the 'meaning-making wall': losing sight of why one is learning.

Motivations such as wanting to raise skills, obtain qualifications, or improve evaluation are powerful in the early stages of self-development, yet once those goals are achieved they can leave a person not knowing what to aim for next.
This often produces burnout or a sense of emptiness; what was once enjoyable learning itself becomes merely a means to an end, and when that end disappears the energy for learning also disappears.

Another aspect of the meaning-making wall is the substitution of personal meaning by others' expectations, such as 'because the boss said so,' 'because people around me are doing it,' or 'to raise my market value.' These appear rational but shift the subject of learning from the self to others' value standards, yielding only temporary drive that fails to support long-term self-development and eventually dulls awareness of what one truly values.

Even when meaning thins, behavior can persist through habituated actions or conformity to environmental expectations, preserving a mere 'sense of continuing.' Without an internal purpose, however, the learning hollows out and self-development mutates into an obligation to produce results or a tool for self-affirmation; this connects to the growth-need discussed in motivation-management chapters.

Self-Determination Theory (Deci & Ryan, 2000) states that spontaneous action requires three elements: autonomy (自律性), competence/sense of efficacy (有能感), and relatedness (関係性). Absence of any one causes loss of meaning-making and a shift to extrinsic control. The same holds for learning: meaning arises only in the continuous cycle of choosing for oneself, understanding with one's own hands, and linking the learning to one's surroundings.

The 'meaning-making wall' (意味づけの壁) is not a drop in motivation but a thinned relationship between the self and learning. In this state, even efficient methods or ample time produce no results because the supporting 'why' is missing.

Social change exacerbates the wall: rapid obsolescence of knowledge shortens the lifespan of learning outcomes, eroding fundamental motivation with the feeling that 'even if I learn it, it will soon be outdated.' The opposite phenomenon—treating perpetual updating itself as the goal—turns learning into an endless competition driven by the anxiety of 'I must always keep updating,' which is itself another form of the meaning-making wall.

Thus the meaning-making wall appears as a misalignment between one's way of living and one's way of learning rather than as a problem of results or external evaluation; therefore the purpose of learning should not be sought externally.
To restore meaning in learning or self-development, reclaim it internally by reflecting on what is important to you and why, rather than seeking it externally.

A practical method for meaning-making: write in one line about what you are learning, such as 'Who does this help?' or 'What would I be happy to be able to do?' Meaning is cultivated not only through thinking but also through small actions.
The 'Energy Wall' (エネルギーの壁) is the counterpart to the 'Busyness Wall' caused by lack of time. It occurs when the driving force needed to keep progressing dries up.
Repeated daily decision-making and interpersonal adjustments fatigue the brain, depleting the fuel required for thinking, concentration, and emotion control. This produces 'decision fatigue' (決断疲れ).
Having the desire to learn after work but being unable to act is a sign of fuel depletion. Attempting to push through this fatigue with willpower or 'guts' often leads to chronic burnout.
Self-development requires not only time management but also energy management.

The Energy Wall can arise from private life as well as work: sleep deprivation, prolonged sitting, unbalanced meals, and personal relationship issues all impair concentration and decision-making ability.

Effective coping strategies include: (1) schedule learning during high-energy periods such as morning or a 15-minute lunch break rather than after work; (2) separate learning into heavy tasks and light tasks (on tired days do only reading or listening; reserve demanding work for energetic days); (3) improve just one of sleep, exercise, or diet rather than trying to fix everything at once.
Energy cannot be increased by willpower alone. Therefore, learning how to manage and handle energy is valuable.

Organizational culture can function as a significant barrier to skill mastery and learning, even though individual members may perceive it as something they cannot influence; however, individuals still have some agency to navigate and overcome it.

Mastering any skill requires substantial time investment, and reaching a proficient level additionally demands accumulated practical experience. When an organizational culture strongly prioritizes short-term results, both securing dedicated time for skill development and obtaining opportunities to gain experience in new or unfamiliar domains become difficult.

A culture unsupportive of learning manifests in everyday comments and attitudes, such as accepting evening study sessions while frowning upon full-day conference attendance during work hours, or reacting to blogging and external speaking with remarks like 'if you have that much free time, come help with this work instead.'

Emphasizing short-term results is not inherently negative; both short-term outcomes and long-term learning are essential for the growth of organizations and individuals. The core problem arises when there is no intentional design to balance the two, causing excessive weight to shift toward the short-term side.

Organizational culture is strongly shaped by management rhythms such as quarterly goal-setting cycles and KPI-driven systems. In such environments, organizations tend to prefer short-term results over long-term learning, so the value of learning is rarely incorporated into evaluation metrics. As a result, many members voluntarily suppress any learning that does not immediately contribute to short-term deliverables.
Workplaces that define 'growth' narrowly as 'skill-up' tend to deprioritize non-quantitative forms of learning, including relationship-building, external knowledge sharing, and personal reflection.

In practice, the task of striking a balance between promoting learning and delivering short-term results typically falls to managers and middle-layer leaders, who experience tension between these two responsibilities. Both are important, and the appropriate balance must be determined according to the specific needs of the organization at that moment.

Short-term results (成果) are supported by long-term growth (成長). Organizations must reliably harvest the 'fruits' of current results while simultaneously attending to long-term growth to enable continuous future harvests. This required balance appears in organizational culture as the accumulated pattern of everyday decision-making.

Company phase affects feasibility of a learning-friendly culture (学習しやすい文化). In the startup/launch phase it can be rational to concentrate first on immediate results rather than immediately building a culture that makes learning easy.
The critical discipline is not missing the moment to reinvest in learning once the situation changes; timing of that reinvestment must not be lost.
Organizational culture is not a matter of good versus evil. It is also a rational mechanism that has emerged from years of successful experience.
What matters is becoming conscious of the influence of that existing cultural mechanism and deliberately reclaiming a learning perspective.

Practical reconnection tactics: verbalize learning in a form that is directly connected to actual work; convert learning outcomes into small, usable deliverables such as memos, checklists, templates, and improvement proposals.
Learning and results should not be treated as opposites. By reconnecting them, cultural barriers become incrementally easier to handle.
